112712.label: Project Title(Chinese)
112712.value: 砂颗粒间接触特性的实验测定

112712.label: Co - Investigator(s)
112712.value: Dr Cavarretta, Ignazio Prof WANG, Jianfeng Jeff

112712.label: Project Objectives
112712.value: To develop the first comprehensive data set and complete understanding of the contact behaviour of sands, through the following detailed objectives: To understand the tangential load-deflection behaviour of particles prior to the onset of sliding. To determine the interactions between tangential and normal loading at all load levels from initial contact to sliding. To examine how contact behaviour varies with particle size, mineralogy, properties and morphology. To investigate any effects of rate of loading or repeated loading on contact behaviour. To characterise the damage to particle surfaces arising from contact loading for a range of load levels. To identify in a systematic manner the effects of ambient humidity and pore fluid on the contact behaviour.

112712.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
112712.value: Discrete Element Analyses are now used extensively in Soil Mechanics, but the contact models that are used for sands under quasi-static loading are relatively simple and are based on surprisingly little data. The aim of the research is to provide the first comprehensive set of data investigating the contact mechanics of sand particles. The proposed research builds on earlier work by the applicants at Imperial College and currently at the City University of Hong Kong in constructing apparatus suitable for such an investigation. Limited previous experiments by the applicants led to the unexpected finding that for soils the normal load-deflection behaviour was dominated by plasticity at very small loads, not elasticity as assumed in the simple models typically used, even if similar behaviour had been seen previously in other materials. However, very little remains known about most key aspects of contact behaviour, and these will be the focus of this research. Perhaps most notable amongst the areas of uncertainty for soils is the behaviour under tangential loading and the interaction of tangential and normal loads. The project will also examine the effects of rate of loading and repeated loading, the influence of pore fluid on contact behaviour and the changes to the morphology of the particles that are caused by contact loading. Most existing work has been restricted to a very narrow range of particle types and so a key objective of the research will be to broaden the sands tested, covering a wide range of mineralogies and particle types and sizes.

112712.label: Realisation of objectives
112712.value: This project has been very successful in achieving all of its objectives and there is none that has not been fully achieved. Indeed, the work has gone even further than anticipated in pushing the boundaries of inter-particle mechanics, accounting for 1) particle damage over a wider range of loads than had been anticipated 2) the presence of cement at the particle contacts, as is common in many natural sands, and 3) a broader range of particle contact types than had been anticipated. The very high quality of the data generated has been largely due to hard work in the early part of the project in improving the inter-particle loading apparatus, enabling tests of a far higher quality than had been initially envisaged could be conducted. These enhancements were centred around, 1) improved quality of displacement measurement through the use of state of the art proximity sensors and the reduction of apparatus flexibility, and 2) the construction of auxiliary loading devices to examine behaviour under higher loads, including the use of high speed imagery to capture the various stages of particle damage 1. To develop the first comprehensive data set and complete understanding of the contact behaviour of sands. This objective was completely achieved with very extensive series of tests on sands of a wide range of mineralogies, including simple quartz sands, carbonate sands of two types, and local Hong King decomposed granite, as well as sands of composite mixed mineralogies. Around 300 tests of different types were carried out. In addition a range of artificial materials were tested as controls; balls made of chrome steel, ceramic and glass, while other tests extended the work sands with cemented contacts and also soils made of granular clay aggregates, the latter in collaborative work with the Politecnico di Bari, Italy. In an exciting development, one of the sands (Eglin sand) was tested in collaborative work with Professor Andrade of Caltech with assistance also from the Politecnico di Milano, Italy; this material has been used by Caltech as Mars surface simulant. The breadth and detail of the knowledge of sand particle mechanics gained is without precedent. 2. To understand the tangential load-deflection behaviour of particles prior to the onset of sliding. All of the soils investigated were examined in detail for their tangential pre-sliding behaviour, since this is the single aspect of inter-particle mechanics about which least is known. As will be seen in the papers the database generated is now very comprehensive, with a complete knowledge of how the inter-particle tangential stiffness decays with increasing displacement. Evidence was also gathered through more sophisticated test procedures about the nature of the displacements, i.e. to what extent they are elastic, due to plastic deformation of the particle surface or due to micro-slipping at the contact, as current theories assume. 3. To determine the interactions between tangential and normal loading at all load levels from initial contact to sliding. A very wide range of normal loads was investigated, for the wide range of particles, allowing a comprehensive investigation of how normal load affects, 1) the pre-sliding stiffness and the rate of decay of that stiffness with displacement, and 2) the value of the inter-particle friction coefficient. 4. To examine how contact behaviour varies with particle size, mineralogy, properties and morphology. The effects of mineralogy were investigated by testing soils of different origins, notably sedimentary carbonate and quartz sands and a decomposed granite from a weathered origin. A variety of sizes was tested, within the limits of the apparatus in terms of load capacity (for the larger particles) and ability to handle the particles and set them in the apparatus (at the small size limit). New techniques were developed that enabled sands down to 1mm to be used, which was particularly challenging. The controlling aspect of morphology was the surface roughness, which was measured by white light interferometry, in collaboration with Dr. Baudet of Hong Kong University. The effects of mineralogy (which controls the elastic modulus), roughness and particle size were analysed within the framework of existing models for particle contact behaviour, that would be used, for example, in Discrete Element Analyses. 5. To investigate any effects of rate of loading or repeated loading on contact behaviour. Rate of loading effects were difficult to investigate, because the scatter of data that occurs naturally between different individual particles would be enough to mask the rate effect being looked for. This problem was overcome by conducting novel step change rate of loading tests, similar to what is done for triaxial tests investigating rate effects within a continuum mechanics framework, changing the velocity stepwise while loading one pair of particles. No significant effects could be found and so the series of tests was limited in extent. Instead, a much more significant affect was found for the influence of pre-loading a particle contact to a higher load prior to shearing at a lower load, a form of “overconsolidation” to use a soil mechanics analogy. 6. To characterise the damage to particle surfaces arising from contact loading for a range of load levels. With the inter-particle loading apparatus, lack of visibility of the particle surfaces together with the rapidity of the occurrence of damage to particles meant that a subsidiary apparatus was built specifically to examine this aspect of behaviour. This apparatus was equipped with a high-speed camera and it also enabled the work to be extended to much higher load levels, to examine the nature of damage at all loads up to catastrophic breakage. Additionally, this auxiliary apparatus allowed the effects of coordination number on the damage patterns to be investigated. 7. To identify in a systematic manner the effects of ambient humidity and pore fluid on the contact behaviour. Control of the environment around the particles was added to the inter-particle loading apparatus, both allowing tests on water immersed particle contacts and also tests on particles with a controlled environmental humidity. Since neither had any significant effect for most soils, this test series was less extensive than was envisaged, apart from the sand from a weathered origin, the decomposed granite, for which the presence of water could have very significant effects.

112712.label: Major findings and research outcome
112712.value: The project has been particularly productive with two PhDs completed, as well as six papers in major journals so far, with others in preparation. The findings were presented in numerous seminars and workshops, notably in a keynote lecture by Coop at the 2014 Cambridge International Symposium on Geomechanics from Micro to Macro). The behaviour of sand particle contacts under normal loading largely obeys an elastic model of behaviour, and so will depend on the particle size (radius) and its mineralogy (which controls the elastic modulus). At smaller loads the roughness of the particles makes the behaviour softer, but again this may be predicted using existing models that account for asperities. At higher load levels the stiffness is no longer affected by the roughness. At the point when severe damage and/or breakage occurs, the nature of the damage depends critically on the shape of the contact between particles (its curvature), and the number of contacts. The presence of cementing changes radically the mode of failure and the load-deflection response. (see papers: Nardelli et al., 2017, Powder Technology; Wang et al., 2017, Géotechnique Letters; Wang & Coop, 2016, Géotechnique; Todisco et al., 2017, Soils and Foundations; Nardelli & Coop, 2014, IS Cambridge; Nardelli & Coop, 2016, Italian National Conference). In shear loading the inter-particle friction resistance is predominately a function of the particle roughness, which is related to its mineralogy and geological origins. At one extreme, soil particles made of aggregated clays formed by tectonic shearing have slickensided surfaces, but the inter-particle friction is more similar to a critical state angle in continuum mechanics than the residual that might have been expected. The friction coefficient between particles reduces slightly with increasing load, while is was found not to be sensitive to loading rate, whether water is present or the ambient humidity, in contrast with the limited data in the literature. Even if the normal loading stiffness may be quite well predicted by existing elastic theory, the tangential stiffness is dramatically overestimated. It is highly dependent on the normal load level, and the current theories do predict this pressure dependency reasonably well, even if the absolute values are incorrect. They also predict well the decay of stiffness with increasing displacement. (see papers: Nardelli et al., 2017, Powder Technology; Nardelli & Coop, 2016, Italian National Conference; Senetakis & Coop, 2015, Experimental Mechanics; Nardelli et al. 2016, Géotechnique Letters).

112712.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
112712.value: Currently DEM analyses are made largely using guessed inter-particle behaviour or using parameters that are optimised to curve fit the behaviour at the macroscopic scale (e.g. triaxial tests). This is the first such comprehensive investigation of the true contact behaviour of soil particles and as such will be invaluable in informing the choice of parameters. Naturally, successful DEM simulation will depend on modelling also other aspects of real particles, such as their shapes, but a detailed knowledge of their contact behaviour is a prerequisite. The further development of this research will therefore be largely in the DEM field. The work also has great potential to shed light on which characteristics of soil particles contribute to which aspect of the macroscopic behaviour (strength, stiffness, compressibility), this having been the topic of considerable speculation throughout the history of soil mechanics. Another key aspect of behaviour that should now be investigated is the dynamic interaction of particles, for example in debris flows, and this is a key element of the Theme-based research project “Understanding Debris Flow Mechanisms and Mitigating Risks for a Sustainable Hong Kong” - Project No. CityU 8779012, for which Coop is an external Co-I.

112712.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
112712.value: Problems in Geotechnical Engineering have traditionally been analysed using similar techniques to those used for most other engineering materials, such as steel or concrete, in that it is treated as a uniform continuous substance – a continuum. Yet the very nature of soils is that they are particulate with a geological, not manmade origin, so when we adopt a continuum based approach the governing equations become extremely complicated and/or not particularly satisfactory. As computing power increases, this may be overcome in the future by analysing soils as individual particles, but at the moment there is very little known about their behaviour as individual particles. This project has largely filled this gap in knowledge by making the first comprehensive investigation of the behaviour at the contacts of two soil particles when they touch each other.

113212.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
113212.value: Intelligent control based on Takagi-Sugeno (T-S) fuzzy models has attracted great attention from control community, and a large volume of results have been published in recent years. These include results on T-S fuzzy system modeling and identification, universal function approximation, stability analysis, and controller synthesis. However, it has been shown most recently that the commonly used T-S fuzzy models can only be used to approximate affine nonlinear systems and thus most of those developed results on T-S fuzzy models can only be applicable to affine nonlinear systems. Then a natural question arises, that is, can one deal with control of general nonlinear systems via a T-S fuzzy model approach? In fact, many critical issues remain to be investigated when dealing with control of general rather than affine nonlinear systems via a T-S fuzzy model approach. For example, what kind of T-S fuzzy models can be used to approximate general nonlinear systems? How can controller synthesis of this kind of T-S fuzzy models be effectively facilitated? Furthermore, suppose a general nonlinear system can be stabilized by an appropriately defined controller, does there exist a fuzzy controller to stabilize it? How can one design the fuzzy controller if it does exist? This project will investigate these issues and develop novel techniques or methodologies for intelligent control of general nonlinear systems via a T-S fuzzy model approach. The outcome of the project is expected to enrich the theoretical foundation of fuzzy model based intelligent control methodology and to provide more tools to control of general nonlinear systems which are expected to be widely utilized in practice. 近年来，基于T-S模糊模型的智能控制方法吸引了控制学科的高度重视，并产出了一批非常重要的结果。其中包括模糊系统建模与辨识，通用函数逼近方法，稳定性分析，以及控制器综合。但是，大部分已有结果只适用于仿射类的非线性系统。当处理更一般的系统，比如非仿射类的非线性系统的控制问题时，很多关键的问题仍有待解决。这些问题包括：哪一类T-S模糊模型可用于逼近一般非线性系统？如何对这类T-S模糊系统进行有效的控制器设计？对于一个可以由适当的控制器镇定的一般非线性系统，是否一定存在相应的模糊控制器去镇定它？如何设计这类模糊控制器？这个项目将主要讨论这些问题，并研究开发出一种新的基于T-S模糊模型的一般非线性系统控制方法。本项目提出的方法将进一步丰富基于模糊模型的控制方法的理论基础，并提供更多处理一般非线性系统控制问题的途径。

113212.label: Major findings and research outcome
113212.value: A number of critical issues on intelligent control of general nonlinear systems via generalized T-S fuzzy models have been investigated. It has been shown that a class of generalized T-S fuzzy models is universal approximators to general nonlinear systems in the sense that they can be used to approximate general nonlinear systems to any degree of accuracy on any compact set of interest. This kind of generalized T-S fuzzy models are very suitable for control synthesis and thus useful in engineering applications. A number of novel approaches to stability analysis and control synthesis of general nonlinear systems have been developed based on the proposed generalized T-S fuzzy models. These approaches are based on various Lyapunov functions such as common, piecewise and fuzzy Lyapunov functions. Both state feedback and output feedback controllers have been developed. Furthermore, the issue of universal fuzzy controllers has been investigated. It is shown that if a general nonlinear system can be stabilized by a smooth controller, there exists a fuzzy controller which can also stabilize the concerned general nonlinear system. Several kinds of general nonlinear systems including both deterministic and stochastic nonlinear systems are considered. Various forms of universal fuzzy controllers have been developed. Finally, the theoretical results have been successfully applied to intelligent control of a couple of benchmark nonlinear systems.

113212.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
113212.value: Although a number of results on intelligent control of general nonlinear systems have been obtained in this project, it is also of interest to investigate further how to develop a systematic way to obtain the structure and parameters of the generalized T-S fuzzy model in describing the concerned general nonlinear system. One way to achieve this objective is to formulate the problem into an optimization problem, ideally a convex optimization problem. This can be one of the future research topics.

113212.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
113212.value: Intelligent control based on Takagi-Sugeno (T-S) fuzzy models has attracted great attention from control community, and a large volume of significant results have been published. However, most of these results are only applicable to affine nonlinear systems and thus many critical issues remain to be investigated when dealing with general instead of affine nonlinear systems. This project has investigated some of those critical issues. In particular, we have investigated the following issues. (i) What kind of T-S fuzzy models can be used to approximate general nonlinear systems? (ii) How can controller synthesis of this kind of T-S fuzzy models be effectively facilitated? (iii) If a general nonlinear system can be stabilized by an appropriately defined controller, does there exist a fuzzy controller to stabilize it? How can one design the fuzzy controller if it does exist? We have obtained a number of results on those issues and developed novel methodologies for controller design of general nonlinear systems via a generalized T-S fuzzy model based approach. The outcome of the project is expected to enrich the theoretical foundation of fuzzy model based control methodology and to provide more tools for control of general nonlinear systems which are expected to be widely utilized in practice.

114012.label: Major findings and research outcome
114012.value: This project aims to utilize the ubiquitous 3G connections for provisions of its users with the most ready and convenient communication medium when other wireless options are inconvenient or impossible at all. In particular, we have carried out the following major research tasks: 1. Designing fundamental protocols to enable 3G bundling and network formulation. This objective has been attained through research on Mobility for HSPA Networks and WiFi deployment (see Journal J4, J9 and J12 and Conference C1) where we consider the 3G/3.5G networks could co-work with WiFi, WiMAX. In addition, we also explore the applications of the fundamental protocols for WiFi and WiMAX network formulations. 2. Optimizing allocation and management of resources such as bandwidth and 3G phone energy Through sensor networking research, we are able to explore the energy efficiency and optimization for the allocation and management on the resources (J1-3 and J8 and J11, C4). We have achieved some fundamemntal contributions on the network resource and user requirement stable matchings and we are the one who first explored three-sided network matching on sensor networks (J13). 3. The related prototypes have been implemented for the optimal deployment for wireless sensor networks; mobile network for long distance trains; WiMAX mesh network and WiFi optimal deployment etc. The results are shown in all the related journals and conference papers as listed in C. In addition, we also extended the research activities on the network coding and security (see J5, J6).

114012.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
114012.value: The three-sided relationship can be found in many scenarios of computer networking systems involving three types of agents. For example, in sensor networks, data are retrieved from data sources (sensors) and forwarded to users through a group of servers. In such three-sided networks, users always prefer to receive the best data services from data sources, data sources would choose servers that are more efficient to deliver their data, and servers try to satisfy more users. Such preferences form a specific cyclic relationship and how to optimally allocate network bandwidth to satisfy preferences of all parties becomes a great challenge. We will make use of this project delivery on Three-sided cyclic network resource matching problem for data sources, servers and users, aiming to find a maximum stable matching for them, where all their preferences are satisfied. We plan to show that the problem of seeking an optimal stable matching with maximum cardinality is NP-hard and propose efficient algorithms for the scenarios of network generation networks such as LTE and data centers for the optimal matchings among bandwidth usage and traffic and movement flows.

114012.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
114012.value: In this project, we proposed a methodology of bundling 3G connections to solve the resource shortage problems. The basic idea of 3G connection bundling is to bring available 3G connections together to form a much broader super-connection and place all valuable resources, such as bandwidth and battery energy under better control. This kind of bundling enables many services that were originally impossible for segregated units. For example, with bundled 3G connections, users could collaborate to continuously stream high-quality videos revealing every perspective of the serviellance scenarios. The outcomes of this project may support other 3G applications, such as mobile TV and gaming, which require prolonged operation time, responsive links and smooth exchanges of large quantities of information.

114112.label: Project Objectives
114112.value: To design an efficient and privacy-preserving third party auditing protocol. The auditing protocol shall meet the following requirements: 1) Confidentiality. It should keep the data confidential against the auditor. 2) Dynamic auditing. It should support the dynamic updates of the data without incurring too much computation or communication cost. 3) Batch auditing. It should be able to support the batch auditing, which combines together multiple auditing requests from multiple owners for batch processing. To design a secure data access control scheme based on CP-ABE (Ciphertext-Policy Attribute-based Encryption) technology. This scheme shall meet the following requirements: 1) Attribute revocation. Whenever there is an attribute revocation, the revoked user should be declined immediately for further data access. 2) Multiple authorities. The scheme should be able to support multiple authorities in the system and prevent users from different authorities from colluding to gain illegal data access. 3) Policy hiding. The data access policies should be kept confidential to cloud servers and data users.

114112.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
114112.value: Cloud storage is an important service of cloud computing, which allows data owners to host their data in the cloud. This new type of data hosting service introduces two major security concerns: 1) Protection of data integrity. Data owners may not fully trust the cloud servers and worry that data stored in the cloud could be corrupted or even removed. 2) Data access control. Data owners may worry that some cloud servers may be dishonest and give data access to the users that do not have access permission for profit gain. The objectives of the project are two-fold. Firstly, to design an efficient and privacy-preserving third party auditing protocol. The auditing protocol shall meet the following requirements: 1) Confidentiality. It should keep the data confidential against the auditor. 2) Dynamic auditing. It should support the dynamic updates of the data without incurring too much computation or communication cost. 3) Batch auditing. It should be able to support the batch auditing, which combines together multiple auditing requests from multiple owners for batch processing. Secondly, to design a secure data access control scheme based on CP-ABE (Ciphertext-Policy Attribute-based Encryption) technology. This scheme shall meet the following requirements: 1) Attribute revocation. Whenever there is an attribute revocation, the revoked user should be declined immediately for further data access. 2) Multiple authorities. The scheme should be able to support multiple authorities in the system and prevent users from different authorities from colluding to gain illegal data access. 3) Policy hiding. The data access policies should be kept confidential to cloud servers and data users. 该项目的目标有两方面。首先，设计一个有效的具有隐私保护功能的第三方审计协议。审计协议应当符合下列要求：1）保密性。它应保证数据对审计师保密。 2）动态审计。 3）批量审计。其次，基于CP-ABE（密文策略属性基加密）技术，设计一个安全的数据访问控制方案。该方案应符合下列要求：1）属性撤销。每当有一个属性被撤销，被撤销属性的用户应立即被拒绝进行进一步的数据访问。 2）多认证机构。访问控制方案应该支持多认证机构的系统，并且防止用户通过不同的认证机构进行勾结，获得非法的数据访问。 3）策略隐藏。数据访问策略应当对云服务器和数据用户保密。

114112.label: Realisation of objectives
114112.value: There are two major objectives: 1) design of an efficient and privacy-preserving third party auditing protocol; and the design of secure data access control schemes for big data in the cloud. As for the first objective, we have developed an efficient and secure dynamic auditing protocol for large scale data storage in cloud computing. The "efficient" means it can efficiently perform the auditing even after the data is modified by the owner; and the "secure" means the auditor cannot obtain or derive any useful information of the data during the auditing process. This paper was published in IEEE Trans on Parallel and Distributed Systems in Sept 2013. It has already become one of the most pupolar papers as posted on the journal's webpage. As for the second objective, we have developed an expressive, efficient and revocable data access Control for cloud storage systems. Traditional CP-ABE method was notorious for poor expressing power for access control policies. This work focuses on expanding the expressing power of CP-ABE method and the efficient revocation algorithm whenever there is any change of user's attributes. This work is further extended to a fine-grained access control method with efficient revocation. We also developed an access control scheme for multi-authority systems. Since in CP-ABE method, there is always an authority that generates and distributes keys for valid users. However, in an environment where a user belongs to multiple organizations and it has keys from multiple authorities, access control becomes a challenging issue. This method focuses on solving the issues of multi-authorities in CP-ABE method. We further developed an efficient access control method with dynamic policy updating for cloud storage systems. With CP-ABE method, it’s always a difficult issue with the change of access policies, which involves huge amount of computational cost to re-encrypt data. This work proposed an efficient method that allows dynamic updating of access policies. Overall, all objectives are successfully achieved.

114512.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
114512.value: Although the birth rate in Hong Kong (HK) ranks among the world’s lowest, life expectancy is among the highest. The proportion of elders in HK is thus increasing and has been projected to reach 24% of the total population by 2031. To tackle the increasing housing demands of the elders, the HK government has focused on a pilot scheme for elderly housing (HKSAR 2010). Nonetheless, among the 1,129,900 elders in HK, more than 50% are currently living in public and subsidized (P/S) housing (Census and Statistics Dept, 2009) with relatively insufficient facilities, and probably without adequate facility support for the elders. The dilapidated housing of the elders implies a poor Quality of Life (QoL), which associates with health and safety problems. The physical environment we live in is a recognized dimension of QoL (World Health Organization QoL Assessment [WHOQOL] Group 1998a), and is likely to be particularly important for domestic elders. Because of limitations in health and mobility, elders spend most of their time at home and depend on facilities and facility management (FM) to compensate for their physical and biological problems, and also to maintain their psychological well-being. ‘Providing purpose-designed housing for elders’ is one of the objectives initiated by the HK Chief Executive in his recent Policy Address (HKSAR 2011). Although the HK government has published the Universal Design Guidebook for residential development in HK (HKHS 2010a), there has been no focus on an integrated FM study covering the construction, social, and psychological disciplines for elderly housing. The literature on FM, caring environmental design, post-occupancy evaluation, building maintenance, and QoL for adults and the elders is extensive, but a study integrating all these aspects for the elders is lacking. The purpose of this research is to enhance the QoL of elders in P/S housing through FM. The objectives are: (1) to factorize FM components in P/S housing and QoL indicators for the elders; (2) to establish FM–QoL relationships for the elders in P/S housing; (3) to develop an integrated FM–QoL model; (4) to verify the model using longitudinal real cases; and (5) to suggest FM guidelines for enhancing the QoL of elders in P/S housing. It is envisaged that the study results will promote the development of a proactive assessment of FM in P/S housing, and enhance the QoL of elders in private housing in the future by disseminating the results to practitioners in the industry. 香港人口老化問題愈見嚴重，預計到2031年，長者人口比例將達到總人口的24%。目前在全港1,129,900名長者中， 逾50%以上的長者居住在公共及政府資助 房屋中 (政府統計處 2009) 。這類房屋大多設施不足，而且缺乏針對長者需要的配套設施。長期生活在這種殘舊的房屋裏，長者生活質素(QoL)持續下降，更引發健康及安全問題。 隨著身體機能逐漸衰退以及活動能力不斷下降，長者大部分時間呆在家中，並且需要適當的設施及設施管理(FM)來解決身體和生理上的問題，并保持心理健康。 因此，香港特區行政長官在最近的施政報告中將「提供特别為長者設計的房屋」作為施政目標之一 (HKSAR 2011)。 本研究的目的是通過設施管理來提升居住在公共及資助房屋裏的長者生活質素。主要目標包括：(1) 分解公共及政府資助房屋的設施管理要素及長者生活質素的因子指標；(2) 研究居住在公共及政府資助房屋裏的長者的設施管理和生活質素(FM–QoL) 的關係；(3) 建立綜合的「設施管理-生活質素」(FM–QoL) 模型；以及(4) 為提升居住在公共及政府資助房屋裏的長者生活質素提出設施管理指引。可以預計，本研究將會主動地推動公共及資助房屋設施管理的評估發展，同時通過將研究成果傳播給建築行業的從業者，進一步提升居住在私人住宅裏的長者生活質量。

114512.label: Realisation of objectives
114512.value: 1. To update the findings in the literature and fine-tune the conceptual model for elders in P/S housing The poverty situation among the elderly intensifies their dependence on public and subsidized (P&S) housing provided by the government. Of the elderly population in the United States in 2010, 9% were living in poverty (DeNavas-Walt et al. 2011); this is also the case for 9.4% of the elderly population in Japan in 2009 (Inagaki 2014), and 32.6% of the elderly population in Hong Kong in 2012 (The Hong Kong Council of Social Service 2012). In fact, 542,600 elderly (38% of the elderly population) are living in P&S housing in Hong Kong (Hong Kong Housing Authority 2014). 2. To factorize FM components and QoL indicators P&S housing is a mass housing program providing affordable living areas for low-income households of a population (Drews 1983). In 1961, the Housing Authority began the development of low-cost housing with a better living environment for Hong Kong residents. It was an improvement in housing design and quality of facilities providing each adult with 35 ft2 of space (Hung 1977). The elderly were initially a low priority, as housing programs originally focused on family needs. Until to 1968, the government built hostel-type accommodation for the elderly, providing 42 ft2 of living space per person with simple emergency alarms, warden services and common rooms, while two to three residents needed to share bathrooms and kitchens (Lai-kwok 2001). In 1988, the Housing Department built Sheltered Housing for the elderly, which was renamed in 1994 as Housing for Senior Citizens. Facilities Management (FM) is responsible for coordinating all efforts to enhance the organization’s ability to compete successfully in a rapidly changing world (Becker 1990). It integrates people such as the elderly in this study, places (public residential buildings) and processes (the facilities), in order to provide an enabling living environment (Springer 2004). Indoor FM components in a residential building can be categorized into three main groups; namely, architecture, building services, and supporting facilities (Leung et al. 2012). The study identified 12 indoor facilities management factors and six QoL domains (i.e., overall QoL, physical and psychological health, independence, social relationship, and living environment). 3. To establish the relationships between FM and QoL of the elders 4. To develop an integrated FMQoL structural equation model Three hundred and sixty five (365) survey data were collected from the elderly in 18 political districts of Hong Kong, while factor analysis and multiple regression analysis were adopted in the data analysis. The results revealed that: (1) space planning, water supply, and non-slip flooring predicts physical health; (2) space planning, furniture, lighting, and water supply improves psychological health of the elderly; (3) color, furniture, and ventilation induces social relationships; (4) living environment is significantly influenced by space planning, furniture, lighting, acoustics, water supply, and non-slip flooring, while temperature negatively affects the living environment; and (5) overall QoL is predicted by distance, furniture, and ventilation. 5. To suggest FM guidelines for enhancing the QoL of the elders in P/S housing based on the model Based on these findings, the study recommends that government review minimum spacing requirements to allow for more physical activity and psychological health of the elderly, while designers and facilities managers are suggested to use warm colors with high levels of illumination, adopt sound insulation materials, install non-flip floor finishes, use single lever-type mixers to provide a stable hot water supply, and pay attention to lighting illuminance and micro-climate settings in P&S flats designed for the elderly.

114512.label: Major findings and research outcome
114512.value: Based on the recommendations of the Working Group on Care for the Elderly in 1994, the government adopted the “aging-in-place” program (Planning Department 2002). Public housing estates adopted Universal Design in order to ensure that the interior of the unit flat and the overall planning of the estate (i.e., the living environment) address the needs of the residents at every stage of their lives (Wai 2006). To meet elderly housing needs, diverse choices of housing schemes were initiated by the Hong Kong government, including the single elderly persons priority scheme for those who wish to live alone, the elderly persons priority scheme for two or more (related or unrelated) elderly willing to live together, and the harmonious families priority scheme (i.e., a combination of families with elderly persons priority scheme and special scheme for families with elderly persons) for families who opt to live with or close to their elderly parents in order to take care of them (Cheng 1999). The study identified 13 indoor facilities management factors and five QoL domains (i.e., overall QoL, physical and psychological health, social relationship, and living environment). The results also reveal that (1) Furniture influence most of the QoL domains, including psychological health, social relationships, living environment and overall quality elderly life; (2) Space planning and Water supply affect their physical /psychological health and living environment; (3) Lighting have positive impact on psychological health and living environment, and Ventilation affect social relationships and overall QoL, and Non-slip flooring influence physical health and living environment; (4) Color, Acoustics and Distance predict elderly social relationships, living environment and overall QoL respectively; and (5) Distance is one of key FM components affect their overall QoL.

114512.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
114512.value: To improve the QoL of the elderly living in P&S housing, for designers and facilities mangers should not only to care about the indoor FM, but also the micro-climate for setting building orientation. The government should review existing spacing requirements to provide more space for physical activity. It is also necessary to efficiently position furniture to give room for social interactions, use warm colors with high levels of illumination in order to make up for visibility deficiencies in the elderly, ensure balance of brightness and colour of lighting, provide valves for automatic regulation of water temperature, install non-slip floor finishes in all the rooms of the elderly’s apartment to prevent the elderly from falling and adopt sound insulating materials in order to manage the effects of noise. The study also provides a useful platform for the further study of indoor facilities, particularly space planning, lighting, ventilation, furniture, etc. for enhancing the QoL of the elderly.

114512.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
114512.value: The growth rate of the aging population raises the demand for and challenges of public and subsidized (P&S) housing for the elderly. This study aims to develop an indoor Facilities Management–Quality of Life (FM–QoL) model for the elderly in P&S housing estates. A questionnaire survey, including five QoL domains and thirteen FM components, were identified. 365 survey data were collected from the elderly in 18 political districts of HK. The results revealed that: (1) space planning, water supply, and non-slip flooring predicts physical health; (2) space planning, furniture, lighting, and water supply improves their psychological health; (3) color, furniture, and ventilation induces social relationships; (4) living environment is significantly influenced by space planning, furniture, lighting, acoustics, water supply, and non-slip flooring, while temperature negatively affects the living environment; and (5) overall QoL is predicted by distance, furniture, and ventilation. Based on these findings, the study recommends that government review minimum spacing requirements to allow for more physical activity in the elderly, while designers and facilities managers need to use warm colors with high levels of illumination, adopt sound insulation materials, install non-slip floor finishes, and pay attention to lighting illuminance and micro-climate settings in P&S flats designed for the elderly.

114612.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
114612.value: Epidemiological evidence has shown that the ambient airborne particle concentration is closely associated with cardio-pulmonary morbidity and mortality. Although these studies draw associations between human health and outdoor air, most personal exposure to particulate matter (PM) occurs indoors. Previous studies have found that human walking indoors results in a short-term, large elevation in particle concentration. Along with infiltration of outdoor air, cooking and smoking, resuspended particles from human activity is one of the primary indoor sources of PM. Particle detachment and resuspension from floors is a very complex progress which depends on micro-scale particle-surface interaction, as well as effects of macro-scale airflow. Although particle resuspension has been investigated via a number of experimental and modeling studies, estimated resuspension rates vary over several orders of magnitude and several important factors are not well understood. In particular, it is hypothesized that electrostatic charge built up during shoe-floor contact and separation may explain the difference between reported resuspension rates for different flooring materials. Also, models have shown that the shoe sole grooved/tread, which influences the airflow velocity in the vicinity of floor, will significantly affect the particle resuspension from the flooring. However, existing analytical models can only be applied for very simple geometry, i.e. circular disk. To understand and mitigate this source of human exposure, it is critical to bridge the knowledge gap. We propose to address the problem via experimental measurements combined with numerical modeling. A mechanical stepping device will be used firstly to determine the effects of different properties of shoes and floorings on the particle resuspension. Electrostatic properties and airflow around grooved shoes as well as the resulting size-resolved particle concentrations will be measured. For the numerical work, an in-house large eddy simulation (LES) based lattice Boltzmann (LB) model with a better capacity to model moving object through immersed boundary (IB) method will be developed and applied to this problem. The models will be verified by experimental data. Our preliminary work indicates that the LB/LES/IB method is a promising approach for this application and will provide the resolution needed to address the research questions. The PI and Co-I are uniquely qualified to conduct the proposed work. The related work they have accomplished and resources available will leverage the project substantially. The results of this study may be used for indoor exposure assessment as well as by other indoor air quality tools.

114612.label: Realisation of objectives
114612.value: 1. To experimentally quantify fundamental electrostatic properties of particles and shoe sole-floor system generated by different shoe soles contacting various flooring materials. A series of experiments were conducted to investigate some important parameters affecting the electrostatic properties including particle seeding, floor materials and shoe soles. Two conditions of the floor samples were tested; unseeded or seeded. Three flooring materials were chosen: linoleum, tile and carpet. All of them are very common for indoor surfaces. Two series of different shoe soles were tested; (i) EVA sole with different groove patterns; (ii) real shoes. For (i), three patterns were chosen; no groove, vertical groove and horizontal groove. The material was ethylene vinyl acetate (EVA is a kind of PVC which is commonly used for shoe soles). For (ii) three common shoe types were tested: slippers (or flip flops), high heels and leather shoes. The test shoe sole materials were EVA for the slippers, polyvinyl chloride (PVC) with iron for the high heels, and raw rubber for the leather shoes. A calibrated DC surface voltmeter was used to measure the accumulated charges on the sole immediately after stomping. Because there is no clearly-defined “voltage” for insulator, instead, the reading of the surface voltmeter gives a quantity proportional to Q/A [in coulombs per cm2]. The detail explanation can be found in the manufacture’s website [trifield.com]. The results of charges per area (Q/A) on the EVA soles are that soles stomping on clean floor consistently give higher Q/A than those floor surfaces seeded with particles. The highest difference, 35 times, occurs at vertical groove for linoleum floor surfaces. It seems that the dust “prevents” electrostatic charge transfer. Inferring from the seeded experiment, it is also interesting to observe that even the same sole material different Q/A are found on the same floor materials for different groove patterns. For triboelectric effect, it depends on how effective the charges are transferred from one surface to another. Inferring from the results, sole with vertical grooves pattern transfers least electrostatic charges than those soles with without groove or horizontal grooves. It is shown that grove pattern affects electrostatic charging. For real shoes, similar observation also hold. It is also observed that linoleum always gives higher Q/A. 2. To study how the pattern of treads/grooves on shoes affecting airflow and resuspension. A manuscript regarding to how airflow affecting resuspension has been submitted to the Building and Environment and the abstract is attached in Part C. For each experiment, the flooring sample was laid on the floor and a volunteer wearing the testing shoe stepped on the sample using a stomping motion (toe and heel hitting at the same time). A multi-channel anemometer (model 1560, Kanomax) was used to measure the airflow induced by the stepdown of the foot at 6 positions along the edge of the shoe. For each experiment, two transducers probes were laid in position on the floor which allowed the airflow jet velocity of two positions to be measured simultaneously. Each location pair was repeated at least 3 times for each shoe. Interesting results are observed. Real Shoe: The results show the stomping induced peak air velocity measured in 6 locations 5 cm from the shoe edge. Air velocities induced by flat shoes were close to twofold of those induced by high heel on both tile and carpet. Flooring type did not have a strong influence on stomping induced air velocity, although the location of the measurement 5 cm from the shoe may explain this result. It is worth noting that flat shoe has three times high bottom area than high heel. The flat shoe resuspended 1.9 to 2.9 times more particles than high heel on carpet, and 1.6 to 3.3 times more on tile flooring. Groove Pattern: Higher velocities were measured at the rear left and right positions outside the shoe sole, than the other measured locations for the horizontal groove and no groove conditions. The vertical groove sole has higher velocities at rear center position than the horizontal and no groove soles, which is consistent with the expected direction of flow. The vertical groove sole also has lower velocities at the lateral positions than the horizontal and no groove soles, although not consistently. The variability in the velocity results may be due to human participants not stepping down exactly the same way in the same location each time. The orientation of the groove pattern showed no statistically significant effect on dust resuspension from carpet and tile, while the shoe with no groove was associated with higher resuspension fractions for particles 5.5 to 10 µm in diameter for both flooring types, and also for particles at 0.8 to 2.5 µm for tile. This result is consistent with the numerical estimation of a higher velocity induced by a smaller gap between the shoe and flooring during the step down process. 3. To develop a new in-house LES based lattice Boltzmann model with a better capacity to model moving object through immersed boundary methodology. Detail modeling development is shown in Part C. A manuscript is under preparation. An in-house LB code has been developed. It is written in C++ language and runs in parallel mode. It includes 4 parts, i.e., (i) the three-dimensional multiple-relaxation-time LB (MRT-LB) model; (ii) LES module to simulate the turbulence; (iii) Lagrangian particle tracking model; (iv) IB module to simulate the moving objects and that is the key point of the project. Brief introduction of each part is given as follows. For (i), the Navier-Stokes (N–S) equations are solved based on the MRT-LB equations with the D3Q19 lattice model. For (ii), in the LB framework the turbulent eddy viscosity is introduced to model the turbulence. The turbulent eddy viscosity is obtained by LES model. In order to improve the LES performance near the wall boundary, the Wall-Adaptive Local Eddy-viscosity (WALE) model is employed. For (iii), the particle momentum equation is solved along with the LB solution by the Euler implicit discretization scheme. For (iv), the IB method is incorporated into the MRT-LB. Two independent meshes are employed: the fixed Cartesian grid which is used by MRT-LB to solve the airflow field, and the Lagrangian points which are used to represent the boundary of moving objects. Through the discrete delta function interpolation, variables on these two meshes can be related to each other. The code has been utilized to simulate the airflow induced by a falling rectangular plate. It is successfully demonstrated that the code can simulate the moving object. 4. To conduct resuspension experiments in a room-size chamber to validate the scale-up of the mechanical stepping device experiments as well as to verify the model in Objective 3. The PI has conducted a series of experiments. The stomping of a shoe induced resuspension and velocity was recorded. The results are compared with mechanical stepping device experiments. The results agree well with each other. The model developed in Objective 3 was also applied to compare the experimental results listed in Objective 2. A rectangular plate of the same dimensions were used. Velocity and resuspension were measured. The modeling results agree well with the experiments.

114612.label: Major findings and research outcome
114612.value: Particle resuspension due to human-walking is clearly demonstrated experimentally and numerically. Results show that floor material, sole material and groove pattern significantly affect particle resuspension. Generally speaking carpet floor gives highest resuspension and the results agree with the literature. Flat shoes enhanced particle resuspension fractions per area compared with high heels on tile. The no groove shoe was associated with higher resuspension fractions than grooved shoes for both flooring materials tested. Shoe sole with vertical grooves pattern transfers least electrostatic charges than those soles with without groove or horizontal grooves. It is shown that grove pattern affects electrostatic charging. Some deposited pathogens can survive from days to even weeks on solid surfaces, pathogens can be resuspensed. Pathogens like bacteria with size ranges from 2 to 10 micrometer can be readily resuspensed. These bacteria can infect human by inhalation. Using UV-C can effectively disinfect these airborne pathogens. Result has been published for a top rank archival journal Building and Environment in 2016 (vol 103, page 99-110). Very interesting findings are reported. It will help engineers to design an effective systems to reduce pathogen infection indoors by various indoor sources such as human resuspension. The results regarding the walking-induced airflow induced have been submitted to Building and Environment. The results for the electrostatic charges will be submitted Feb 2017. A final draft is attached in Part C. The result for Lattice Boltzmann Modeling (LBM) development is under-preparation. Now data is being analyzed and it should be submitted by June (2017). It is also attached in Part C. In addition two conference papers have been published and the details are shown below: Alvin C.K. Lai, Yilin Tian, Andrea R. Ferro. Experimental Study of the effect of shoe type on walking-induced resuspension. Dust 2016, 2nd International Conference on Atmospheric Dust, Taranto, Italy 12-17 June, 2016. Alvin C.K. Lai. A Numerical Study on Effectiveness of Upper-Room Ultraviolet Germicidal Irradiation System in a Simulated Hospital Ward. 2nd Asia Conference Civil, Material & Environmental Sciences, Tokyo, Japan 15-17 March, 2013.

114612.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
114612.value: The current work achieves all the planned objectives. Both experimental measurements and numerical modeling development have generated many useful results. The PI has published a paper on modeling UV disinfection for indoors in the journal Building and Environment. Future development includes conducting resuspension of bacteria and measuring the disinfection efficiency under various UV configurations. The results are very useful and it can be used to validate the previous model and to estimate infection risk. We have collected surface charges for different soles. Future work can measure airborne charges due to walking for different soles/floor materials. Groove pattern of the sole has never been studied before this work. The results can be used to explain the observed resuspension in the literature. For the numerical work, an in-house large eddy simulation (LES) based lattice Boltzmann (LB) model with a better capacity to model moving object through immersed boundary (IB) method has been developed. Immersed boundary method is computational efficient to model moving objects. This model has great potential to model more realistic resuspension events due to human moving, i.e. different stomping patterns.

114612.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
114612.value: Much scientific evidence has shown that the ambient airborne particle concentration is closely associated with heart disease. Although these studies draw associations between human health and outdoor air, most personal exposure to particulate matter (PM) occurs indoors. Previous studies have found that human walking indoors results in a short-term, large elevation in particle concentration. This study is the first to investigate the shoe effect experimentally. The experiments were conducted in a controlled environmental chamber and a human participant performed prescribed stomping activity. Stomping-induced air velocity was measured at 6 locations along the edge of the shoe. Regarding shoe type, flat shoes enhanced particle resuspension fractions compared with high heels on tile, while no difference between the shoe types was observed on carpet. The no groove shoe was associated with higher resuspension fractions than grooved shoes for both flooring materials tested. Resuspension fractions, which increased with particle size, were found to be within the range of previous studies. A new simulation model has been developed. It can model a moving object successfully. This model is computational more efficient than the previous models and has great potential for modeling more realistic resuspension events.

114712.value: 道砟軌道系統是最重要的鐵路運輸系統之一。鑒於鐵路安全的重要性，有工業應用的研究工作早已開展。目前的鐵路軌道檢測系統非常全面，用於檢測鐵軌的水平，對齊，軌距和起皺的方法快速而又有效。然而，檢測工作狀態下的鐵路軌枕連同底下的道砟仍依賴目視檢查。目視檢查對於檢測“表面”的損傷表現良好。而對於隱藏的損傷（如混凝土軌枕底下的裂縫以及位於軌枕受力區域底下或者道床砟肩的道砟損傷），要透過目視檢查檢測這些損傷是極其困難的。但這些損傷會影響軌道的穩定性並且使軌道的工作性能惡化。在道砟軌道中，道砟保持軌枕在合適的位置，軌枕支撐鐵軌。如果軌枕或道砟有任何損傷，鐵路-軌枕-道砟系統的剛度會相應減小。這會改變系統的動態特性，這種變化能從原位軌枕的振動數據中反應出來。通過檢測目標系統的振動狀態來做損傷識別的概念並不新。已經有文獻研究關於使用原位軌枕的振動數據定量軌枕或是道砟的剛度。隨著模態測試技術的發展，準確的測出動態特性（如，固有頻率和振型）的變化不難。然而，這種變化可能是由軌枕損傷導致也可能是由道砟損傷導致。除了抬起軌枕外，現在沒有方法能分類損傷類別。這是振動損傷識別方法應用於道砟軌道的最大障礙。擬建項目的主要目標之一就是克服這個困難，並且制定切實可行的方法，能夠給工程師以及檢查員在目視檢查中可靠地提供有關每一根混凝土軌枕和底下道砟“健康”的資料。

114712.label: Realisation of objectives
114712.value: All objectives in this project were completed. At the beginning of the project, several modeling methods were developed for capturing the vibration characteristics of the rail-sleeper-ballast system with particular considerations when there is damage on the ballast and/or sleeper. To capture the behavior of ballast under train load (large amplitude vibration), and nonlinear model was also developed in this project (Objective 1). Different classes of models were employed to model different damages on the rail-sleeper-ballast system. The new Bayesian methodology was developed for calculating the probability of different model classes for the identification of the type of damage on the system (Objective 2). Once the model class is selected (by selecting the one with the highest probability), the damage location and extend can be estimated by following the Bayesian model updating method as part of the newly developed Bayesian methodology (Objective 4). To ensure the newly developed methodology is practical, a series of experimental tests were carried out for the verification of the newly developed methodology (Objective 4). In order to implement the proposed methodology, the method statement was completed (Objective 5). A more detail description of various objectives and the corresponding publications are given below. About objective 1, several modeling methods were developed for capturing the behavior of ballast and sleeper damages at various locations of the rail-sleeper-ballast system. The basic linear model was presented in the journal paper (Lam, Hu & Wong 2014) and a series of conference papers (Hu & Lam 2013; Lam, Hu & Yang 2013). The extension of the basic linear model to nonlinear model was presented in the conference paper (Lam, Alabi & Zhang). A special class of models for handling sleeper damage was presented in the conference paper (Lam, Hu & Alabi 2016). About objectives 2 and 3, a new MCMC-based Bayesian methodology (including model updating and model class selection) was developed. The outstanding advantage of the newly developed method is to calculate the probability of a model class conditional on a set of measured data even when the levels of measurement noise and modeling error are high (i.e., under the situation of unidentifiable cases). The new method utilizing the Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation for generating a set of samples in the important region of the parameter space for the approximation of the posterior probability density function (PDF) of the damage. The formulation of the new MCMC-based Bayesian methodology is one of the most important contribution of this project. It must be pointed out that this MCMC-based Bayesian methodology can be easily extended for solving other system identification problems (e.g., modal identification and model updating of buildings and bridges). Part of the formulations of the newly developed Bayesian methodology and its application in railway safety were presented in the journal paper (Lam, Hu & Wong 2014) and a series of conference papers (Hu & Lam 2014; Lam, Alabi & Hu 2016; Lam, Hu & Alabi 2016). The extension of this Bayesian methodology in the structural damage detection of transmission tower was reported in two journal papers (Yang & Lam 2013; Lam & Yang 2015) and a conference paper (Yang & Lam 2013a). Instead of following the probability theory, model updating can be carried out by utilizing artificial neural network (ann). Two conference papers were published by following this direction (Wong & Lam 2013; Wong & Lam 2014). The extension of the proposed Bayesian methodology in the detection of joint damages of steel frame structures was reported in a conference paper (Peng & Lam 2013). About objective 4, a comprehensive series of tests were carried out for measuring vibration data for the verification of the proposed modeling method, Bayesian methodology, and damage detection method. It must be pointed out that a new measurement technique, which consists of a specify hardcopy and software package together with a particular designed experimental procedure, was developed for the vibration test of the rail-sleeper-ballast system. Most of the tests were performed in the in-door test panel (particular designed for this project with the in-kind support form MTR Corporation Limited), while some tests were carried out in real ballasted tracks (with the full support from MTR Corporation Limited). The verifications were reported in the journal paper (Lam, Hu & Wong 2014) and some conference papers including (Hu & Lam 2013; Hu & Lam 2014; Lam, Alabi & Zhang 2014; Lam, Alabi & Hu 2016). The new measurement technique was extended for the vibration measurement of other vibration sensitive structural systems, such as wind turbines and metal roofing systems. The extension of this new measurement technique was reported in two journal papers (Peng & Lam 2016; Peng, Lam & Lee 2016) and two conference papers (Pang & Lam 2015; Lam & Hu 2016). About objective 5, the method statements of the proposed methodology were completed. The implementation procedures for the proposed methodology were reported in sections 3.2.3 and 5.2 of the PhD thesis (Hu 2015). This document was also submitted to MTR Corporation Limited. The outputs of this project have great impact to the area of railway safety especially for ballasted track systems. With the outstanding contributions to the field, the PI (Dr. Lam) was invited to give a Keynote in the Jiangsu Mechanics Conference (Lam 2015) and an invited seminar in the 2nd Cross-Strait Symposium on Dynamic Systems and Vibration (Lam 2012). Most analytical development and experimental works in this project are reported also in the PhD thesis (Hu Qin 2015). Part of the nonlinear modeling work in this project will be appear in the PhD thesis of ALABI Stephen Adeyemi (expected graduation on Mar 2017). The measurement technique developed in this project also helped the completion of the PhD thesis (Peng 2016). 114712.label: Major findings and research outcome
114712.value: The research findings and outcomes are summarized in the following. (1) In this project, several new modeling methods for capturing the vibration characteristics of rail-sleeper-ballast system were developed with particular consideration in their possible application in ballasted track damage detection. (2) With these developed classes of models (each model class for a given damage type), the newly developed Bayesian methodology can be used to (a) select the most plausible model class (by calculating the probability of all model classes) and so as the identify the type of damage; and (b) estimate the damage location and extent by updating the uncertain parameters of the selected model class. It is well-known that the uncertainty of ballast properties is very high (owing to their random nature). Under such situation, model updating problems are usually classified as unidentifiable. Most existing model updating method cannot be used for unidentifiable model updating problems. To overcome this problem, the newly developed Bayesian approach adopts the Markov chain Monte Carlo simulation in generating a set of samples in the important region of the parameter space for the approximation of the posterior PDF of uncertain parameters (e.g., damage location and extents). The newly developed Bayesian methodology can be easily extended for solving other system identification problems. (3) To verify the newly developed methodology, a series of experiments were carried out. The tests including experiments in the in-door test panel (under well controlled environment) and out-door field (existing ballasted tracks from MTR). The measured set of data (published in various journals and conferences) provide important information for testing methods from other researchers. (4) In this project, a new measurement technique was developed for the vibration measurement of ballasted track system. This new measurement technique can be extended for the vibration test of various types of structural systems. (5) The method statement of the proposed methodology was developed. This is important for the implementation of the method in the future.

114712.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
114712.value: One of the main contributions of this project is the development of the Bayesian methodology for model class selection and model updating. In this project, the methodology was already extended to various fields of applications. The methodology can certainly be extended and used in other fields. For example, modal identification of structural systems based on a set or multiple sets of measured vibration data. Furthermore, it is also possible to further develop the methodology for reliability analysis of structural systems under earthquake or typhoon. It must be pointed out that the knowledge in the modeling of the rail-sleeper-ballast system forms a key element in the analysis of train-track coupled vibration. The research findings in this project are essential in the future development of modeling methods for train-track vibration simulation. This can then be applied in the study of human comfort in the train vehicle; train induced vibration to the surrounding structures; train-bridge vibration; train suspension system; damage detection of train and track. The study of train-track coupled vibration is one of the future research direction of the PI.

114712.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
114712.value: The current railway track monitoring system is comprehensive. Fast and efficient methods are available for monitoring of railway level and alignment, rail gauges, corrugation, etc. However, the monitoring of the functional condition of railway sleepers together with the underlying ballast still heavily relies on visual inspection. It is clear that visual inspection is good in detecting “surface” damage. For hidden defects, such as cracks at the bottom of the concrete sleeper and the ballast defects under the sleeper loading area and/or ballast shoulder, which can affect track stability and deteriorate riding quality, are extremely difficult, if not impossible, to be detected through visual inspection. The idea of damage detection by monitoring the vibration of the target system is not new. However, the changes in vibration characteristics can be induced by sleeper damage and/or ballast defect, and there is no existing method that can be used to classify the types of defects without lifting up the sleeper. This project developed a practical method to overcome this difficulty and to provide valuable information about the “health” status of each concrete sleeper and the underlying ballast to engineers and inspectors during visual inspection.

115112.label: Project Objectives
115112.value: We will investigate the consistency problem due to different user movement patterns. We will formally model this problem and quantify the amount of inconsistencies for each type of movement pattern. We will study the trade-offs between the effective resolution of inconsistencies and load balancing of users among multiple servers. We will develop an optimization framework to minimize inconsistency. We will investigate the drift in server loading due to the processing and network delays. We will also study how it affects the accuracy of the load balancing solutions produced by load balancing methods. We will develop methods to compensate for the drift in server loading. We will extensively evaluate the performance of our approach in a simulated environment under various conditions.

115112.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
115112.value: 分布式交互应用（DIAs）是指基于互联网并且强调实时交互的应用。近年来，随着在线游戏、分布式虚拟环境和协同设计系统等一系列分布式交 互应用的成功，它 们越来越受到业界的关注。由于这些应用能够被任意的能连到互联网的用户使用，它们将面对一个重要问题——当用户数量不断增长时，怎样才能 确保服务质量不下 降？对于满足用户所期望的实时交互来说，分布式交互应用具有比非实时的互联网应用更严格的响应时间限制。 过去十年里我们其中一个研究重点是运用基于多服务器的负载均衡技术来解决分布式交互应用的可扩展性问题。在初期 我们已经开发出高效的负载均衡算法来解决服务器过载的问题。我们意识到，虽然我们能够有效的解决服务器过载问题，但是负载均衡过程自身也 会引入额外的处理 延迟和服务器间通信的延迟。这些延迟会导致两个问题，一个是用户间交互引发的一致性问题，另一个是服务器负载变动引发的负载均衡方案的准 确性问题。 在本项目中我们将探究这两个问题。为了解决一致性问题，我们将研究去除不一致性的方案和服务器负载均衡的方案之间的优化问 题。本着提高分布式交互式应用的服务质量和用户体验的目的，我们将寻找最优的负载分区方案以便最小化由于网络延迟导致的不一致性，同时确 保每个服务器上的 负载低于一个给定的阀值。为了解决负载均衡方案的准确性问题，我们将开发一种延迟校正方法来补偿由于处理和网络延迟造成的服务器负载变 动。我们提出的方法 对于分布式交互应用的负载均衡问题来说是新颖的。本项目将引领我们用不同的角度来分析分布式交互应用的负载均衡问题，给多服务器分布式交 互应用的设计带来 显著和长远的影响。

115112.label: Realisation of objectives
115112.value: In this project, we first performed a thorough analysis on user movement patterns in the virtual environment (VE). Our DVE model represents the whole VE as regular square cells. Each cell is a basic unit and served by only one server. The number of users within the cell represents the load of this cell. Each server would manage one or more cells. Hence, the total number of users in all cells managed by a server represents the total amount of load managed by this server. On the other hand, the users in the VE may interact with each other. The delay between two interacting users determines the view inconsistency, and is defined by the delays between each user’s PC and their servers together with the delay between the two servers serving the two users. Our main objective of this project is to develop an optimization approach to optimize between the server load balancing problem and the user inconsistency problem. To do this, we first categorized user movements within and across cells in the VE into three main types so that we could analytically model the inconsistencies produced as a result of different types of movements. Type I refers to a user’s movement within the current cell, which will affect other users mainly within the current cell. Type II refers to a user moving from the current cell to an adjacent cell, which will affect other users in the current cell as well as those in the adjacent cell. Type III refers to a user teleporting into or out of the current cell, and we only need to consider the affected users located in the current cell. With these three types of user movements, we could then estimate the amount of view inconsistency caused by the movement of a single user to the other users in each single time step. By integrating the estimation over time for all users, we could then approximate the scale of the view inconsistency problem and the total number of update messages needed to be transmitted among the servers of the DVE. The scale of this view inconsistency problem depends on the server-server latencies as well as the client-server latencies. In order to be able to minimize both the server workload and the view inconsistency, we constructed a weighted undirected graph. In this graph, each node represents a server and its weight represents the workload of the server. Each edge of the graph connects two nodes and the weight of the edge represents the amount of view inconsistency between the two nodes. With this weighted undirected graph, we could then solve our optimization problem in two steps. The first step is to use a Knapsack-based partitioning algorithm to cluster all the cells in the VE into a number of partitions, where this number is equal to the number of servers available in the DVE. The second step is then to assign each partition to an appropriate server such that the total amount of view inconsistency is minimized, while the load differences among the servers are also minimized. Our results showed that the proposed method was very efficient and had the lowest average number of overloaded servers over time, compared with the other methods. Please refer to our paper “On View Consistency in Multi-Server Distributed Virtual Environments” for details. We further investigated the server workload drifting problem. In a DVE system where all the local servers are placed in the same site, the communication delay among the servers may be neglected. However, in a large scale DVE system, users may be accessing the service from around the world, and the local servers may need to be physically distributed. In this situation, the communication delay among the local servers may no longer be neglected. The existence of this network delay causes two accuracy problems for a load balancing method. The first problem is the server workload drifting problem. As there is a time gap between the moment when a local server sends its load information to the central server and the moment that this local server receives the cell migration information from the central server, the latest load of this local server may be very different from the one used by the central server to compute the cell migration information. This server workload drifting problem significantly affects the effectiveness of the load balancing process. We proposed two approaches to address this problem. One was for each local server to compute the workload drifting between its lasting workload reporting to the central server and when it received the load balancing information from the central server. It then uniformly redistributed the load difference to its adjacent servers. The second was to track the movement of the users at the partition boundaries. If these users disappeared from the partition when the server received the load balancing information, we could then assume that they moved to the adjacent partitions. This way, we could have a much better picture on load migration during the server communication delay and use this information to adjust the cell migration information for each server, sent by the central server. The second problem is that if the communication delay among the servers is comparable to the interval between two consecutive load balancing processes, the previous load balancing process may not have been completed when the central server begins a new load balancing process. This will cause significant load fluctuation. To address this problem, we need to make sure that the interval between any two consecutive load balancing processes is longer than the time needed to complete a load balancing process. Please refer to our paper “Dynamic Load Balancing in Distributed Virtual Environments using Heat Diffusion” for details. In this project, we additionally studied two problems related to having a large number of users in a DVE. The first one was also the scalability problem, but a cloud-based environment. We investigated both horizontal scaling and vertical scaling. In horizontal scaling, we considered adding (when under-provisioned) or removing (when over-provisioned) servers to/from the cloud to match the load requirement. In vertical scaling, we considered scaling up (when under-provisioned) or scaling down (when over-provisioned) the server capacity to match the load requirement. We showed that the performance of these two schemes performed better than existing approaches. Please refer to our paper “Dynamic Resource Management in Cloud-based Distributed Virtual Environments” for details. The second one was on tracking user movements. In order to better model user movements in a DVE, we tried to track real user movements. To do this, we developed a very efficient method for tracking human, using the locality sensitive histograms (LSHs). Please refer to “Robust Object Tracking via Locality Sensitive Histograms” for details. We then developed a multi-person tracking method by combining particle filters and reciprocal velocity obstacles. Please refer to “Leveraging Long-Term Predictions and Online-Learning in Agent-based Multiple Person tracking” for details. As a future work, we are following up on the tracking work, and currently trying to determine the interaction behaviors of a crowd of people. We believe that if we can categorize crowd motions and behaviors, we can use them to model user interaction behaviors in the DVE more accurately and effectively.
