244712.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
244712.value: Research in the west on economic globalization highlighted the continual social polarization of global cities, accompanying which is the spatial polarization process. Under such a context, ‘urban ghettos’ exhibit distinctive features, including: casualization of employment, unemployment and stigmatization. In Hong Kong, the emergence of Tin Shui Wai (TSW), which is a new town developed since the early 1990s, points to the possibility of such a partitioning effect. TSW is divided into north and south with the south being developed in the first phase. The problems that TSW south has faced have been intensified in the north where 85% of the population is of low income and there is a serious lack of commercial and industrial activities, and community facilities. Yuen Long, (TSW is part of this larger district) has been occupying top positions among districts in predictors or actual figures of social problems. In response to the severity of the “problems’ of TSW North (TSWN), the Hong Kong Government has been funding community development projects that target at developing social capital of the community. Social capital, community development, poverty alleviation and their interactions constitute the conceptual framework of this research. Following the recommendations of the GRF reviewers, the PI and Co-I conducted a pilot study to construct a local scale for measuring social capital in 2011. The depth interviews with residents and focus group meetings with social workers were conducted prior to the community survey. The findings were used to review and reformulate the questionnaire. A pilot study was then conducted with a random sample of 130 respondents. Although small-scale, the quantitative study achieved the objective of constructing a local tool for measuring social capital in TSWN. This proposed study is to repeat the pilot study with a larger sample in order to validate this new measurement tool and confirm the unique composition of social capital identified by the pilot study. A case study of four community development projects that have been applying distinctive strategies for advocacy, welfare service provision, neighbourhood organization and volunteer networks will be conducted to explore in detail the strategies they have applied that involve the use of social capital in the community in general and for poverty alleviation in particular. The long term significance of this study lies in its dual theoretical and practical relevance with respect to the development of a localized measurement tool of social capital and community development of TSWN.

244712.label: Realisation of objectives
244712.value: The two objectives of the research have, without doubt, been completely realized. Regarding the Objective 1, a community survey of social capital was carried out in Tin Shui Wai North (TSWN) from June to December 2013. The survey adopted a cross-sectional design and measured the social capital using the Social Capital Questionnaire (SCQ) developed by Onyx & Bullen (2000, 2005). The translation of the SCQ from English to Chinese followed a typical back-and-forth process before the final version was adopted. This version of the SCQ-Chinese (SCQ-C) was pilot tested on a convenient random sample of 151 respondents from the same community to establish the validity of the questions, the linguistic and conceptual equivalence of the SCQ-C with the original version and the clarity of the questions to the Cantonese-speaking Chinese respondents. Amendments were made to two questions. A survey involving 1,171 samples was then conducted to validate the scale in TSWN. The construct validity of SCQ-C was confirmed through statistical tests, including Cronbach’s alpha, confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling, using AMOS Version 21. The various statistics (i.e., Cronbach’s alpha = 0.819, comparative fit index = 0.820, root mean square error of approximation = 0.048 and variance extracted = 36.97%) indicated that the scale was robust. In addition, correlation between SCQ-C and the Lin’s scale, which helps to determine the quality of the newly constructed scale and the indigenization of such scale, were run. The respective correlations were noted to be statistically significant with an acceptable level of correlation obtained (R=0.444, p<0.01 when correlated with the SCQ and R=0.274, p<0.01 when correlated with the Lin’s scale). Regarding Objective 2, it has been achieved by conducting qualitative interviews with forty-eight residents who are service users of four community development projects selected for this study, to explore in detail their experiences in using the services, and problems they have encountered in mobilising the support and resources that are needed for poverty alleviation. Twelve residents from each community, two from each of the following categories: the unemployed/underemployed, single mothers, CSSA recipients, new arrivals from mainland China, racial minorities and the elderly were sampled and were referred by social workers. In addition, individual depth interviews were conducted with eight social workers working for these projects to identify the strategies they have applied that involve the use of social capital in the community.

244712.label: Major findings and research outcome
244712.value: Regarding the survey on social capital in Tin Shui Wai North, Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) was conducted to verify the 8-factor, 34-item SCQ-C. A stable model of general social capital was identified via hierarchical factor analysis, as specified by Onyx and Bullen (2000). The General Social Capital score was 2.22 out of 4, based on the mean scores of 7 factors. Among these 7 factors, ‘tolerance of diversity’ rated the highest (2.76) followed by ‘feelings of trust and safety’ (2.71) and ‘proactivity in a social context’ (2.60). ‘Participation in the local community’ (1.34) was the lowest, followed by ‘neighbourhood connections’ (2.02). These factor mean scores highlighted the relative weights of the different elements of social capital in the community. The construct validity of the SCQ-C was confirmed through statistical tests, including Cronbach’s alpha to estimate internal consistency among items, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to examine causation between sets of latent and observed variables, and structural equation modeling to determine the validity of multiple relationships among variables using AMOS Version 21. The tests confirmed that the scale was robust: Cronbach’s alpha = 0.819, only slightly lower when compared with the original SCQ (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.84); comparative fit index = 0.820, root mean square error of approximation = 0.048, variance extracted = 36.97%. The item-total correlations were in the relatively acceptable range (r+0.475-0.132). Regarding the findings on community development strategies employed by social workers to develop social capital, the projects examined all considered social capital as highly relevant to their work. Strategies that facilitated the development of bonding social capital included a direct approach of providing material benefits, organizing group purchasing, using existing networks of individuals, developing new community networks, mobilizing assets in terms of individual skills and talents to serve the community, and initiating community economic development (CED). Strategies to develop bridging social capital adopted included mobilizing resources such as commercial medical groups, private companies and higher-income communities in TSW South to deliver free services or make donation of goods. The involvement of the estate management offices of the public housing estates in TSWN to offer support in terms of access to space for residents’ meetings and activities, and in referring families in need to social workers was one example of strategies to mobilize linking social capital. Another source of government resource was the estate management advisory committees (EMACs) for each public housing estate, which the Housing Department had organized.

244712.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
244712.value: This research study has successfully validated the Social Capital Questionnaire – Chinese (SCQ-C) which can be modified for use in other Chinese communities such as the China, Taiwan and Singapore. The development of a reliable measurement tool of social capital has implications for social work and health care practice. First, in view of the paucity of research findings related to instruments assessing social capital in Chinese people and the community, the validation of the SCQ-C will enable Chinese social and health workers to assess the social capital of individuals and communities. Second, the results of this study also provide a database for future comparisons across communities. Third, in view of the increasing number of social service and health development projects targeted at developing social capital of neighbourhoods, the measurement of social capital can provide more objective outcome measures for helping professions. This study has also identified strategies to develop different types of social capital. It has offered many recommendations which include offering financial subsidies for innovative services, bridging the gaps between residents from different backgrounds, forming collaborations among community organisations, facilitating community participation through encouraging local activities and addressing distrust among residents.

244712.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
244712.value: The two objectives of the research have been realized. A survey involving 1,171 samples was conducted to validate the Social Capital Questionnaire – Chinese (SCQ-C) in Tin Shui Wai North. The construct validity of SCQ-C was confirmed through statistical tests the results of which indicated that the scale was robust. The validated SCQ-C can be modified for use in other Chinese communities. It will enable Chinese social and health workers to assess the social capital of individuals and communities. The results of this study also provide a database for future comparisons across communities, and the measurement of social capital can provide more objective outcome measures for helping professions. In order to identify strategies to develop different types of social capital, forty-eight service users of and eight social workers from the four community development projects selected for this study were interviewed. The projects examined all considered social capital as highly relevant to their work. The study has offered recommendations on strategies that facilitated the development of bonding, bridging and linking social capital. From the perspective of improving people’s livelihood in a remote community, it seems clear that the link between social capital and community development has to be strengthened.

245112.label: Realisation of objectives
245112.value: This is the completion report of my first GRF grant, active from the period 1 January 2013 to 30 June 2015. I have successfully achieved FOUR out of five objectives: (1) To complete a book length manuscript: 100% I have finished a lengthy book manuscript. Book proposals have been to various publishers. I have received a letter of interest from Palgrave Macmillan. (2) To examine the diverse representations of the neighbour: 100% I read the world of Jane Austen through the evolutionary lens and came up with a coherent framework to discuss the problem of the neighbour, neighborliness, kin conflicts, and neighbour-love. (3) To review Austen’s idea of the neighbour in the light of various discourses, and find out if Austen can offer different models of the (female) neighbour as a performative subject, a diplomatic mediator, and a political citizen: 100% With reference to the ongoing dialogues between religion and evolutionary theories, I analyzed the conflicts between self-selection, kin concern, reciprocal neighborliness, and group altruism in the world of Jane Austen. (4) To formulate Austen’s ideological reconstruction of neighbourliness, and the ethical and political implications of the self-neighbour relation: 100% This project argues that Jane Austen cherishes a boundary-sensitive understanding of neighbor-love. Her outlook goes well with the designated gender roles, social practices, and the polite gentry culture in the Regency era. (5) To explore the role of the neighbour in Austen’s adaptations: 10% I decided to scale down the project so the film part is minimalized in this study. Overall performance Research I have successfully achieved Objectives 1-4, and used a coherent and interesting angle to examine the concept of altruism, neighbourliness, and neighbour-love in the world and works of Jane Austen. Conference Supported by this grant, I presented two conference papers at the University of Cambridge and the University of Oxford. 1. “Pride and Prejudice: Character Assassination and Revenge.” Paper presented at at the 200th year of Pride and Prejudice Conference on 22 June 2013 at the University of Cambridge. 2. “Local Celebrity and the World of Jane Austen.” Paper presented at the 3rd Global Conference –Celebrity: Exploring Critical Issues. University of Oxford (Mansfield College). July 22, 2014. I attended an additional conference to present my research findings in Japan in 2015. 3. “Neighbor Networks and Sense and Sensibility.” Paper presented at the International Symposium on Language, Linguistics, Literature and Education Conference. Osaka, Japan. August 26, 2015. Public Talk: Hong Kong Arts Festival Plus Event I gave a talk “The World of Jane Austen” on 7 March 2015 as a part of the Hong Kong Arts Festival Plus Event. The talk went with the Gate Theatre’s production of Pride and Prejudice in the same month, and the aim was to rouse public interest in Austen. I included a lot of historical information, dwelling on Austen’s representation of the neighbourly culture in Pride and Prejudice. Problems Encountered: It is difficult to incorporate evolutionary theories, biographical approaches, textual analysis, socio-historical studies with film studies in this project. As a result, I removed the film part after 2014.

245112.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
245112.value: My book argues that even though every man for himself is the ultimate aim and radical altruism is hard to find, no society can exist without varying degrees of altruism. Since altruistic acts involve a cost, Jane Austen’s approach is to defend a boundary-sensitive notion of other-mindedness. On the question of resource allocation, both kin and non-kin have an important place in her world. Jane Austen sees that one should invest in the family, the Church, the neighborhood, the nation, and personal relationships. At the same time, there are all kinds of factors to be considered in one’s investment efforts, ranging from genetic relatedness, personal and psychological proximity, gender roles, class difference, and need-based, group-based, or merit-based assistance. In her novels, she puts forward the view that although egoism is highly problematic, altruism is not without its dark side. Readers are encouraged to ponder the (expanding) circles of human connections to re-interpret from time to time the truly desirable prosocial, cooperative behaviors that can benefit a particular community. From kin care, mate preference, and neighborly interactions to civic duty, Jane Austen always have something new to communicate to her readers, past and present.

245212.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
245212.value: The overarching aim of this project is to construct a historical narrative of social and cultural exchange among native and non-native peoples in Amuria during the early modern period, roughly from 1600 to 1910. The term “Amuria” will denote a geographical and cultural zone including the areas presently known as Northeast China and Southeastern Siberia. This concept itself will be a significant cornerstone of the project, emphasizing characteristics such as migration patterns and kinship networks rather than political borders. It also stresses that the tributary streams of the Amur River (Heilongjiang) acted alternately as boundaries circumscribing the activity zones of discrete communities, and as conduits of contact between them. The project will moreover highlight the co-existence of multiple polities and societies in this spatial arena, as represented by not only the multitude of indigenous populations, but also visitors and migrants from neighboring regions. Interactions between these groups fueled social and cultural synergy that in turn shaped their political and economic relationships with one another, as well as with the non-indigenous states that competed to exert their absolute authority over Amuria. By including as many perspectives as extant sources will yield, the resulting research outputs, a monograph and a wiki-based website, will make two significant contributions to historiographical and pedagogical paradigms. The first innovation of this project is to enrich as-yet underexplored conceptions of indigeneity in Amuria, and then put forth fresh parameters for determining varying degrees of indigenous self-identification and external recognition of indigenous status through social, political, and legal means in this region. To do so, this study will utilize tools of analyzing native history, such as ethnographical fieldwork, and of examining local history in both textual and non-textual forms. The first of two research stages will be collecting published works. The second stage will be acquiring resources that are only accessible at or near their places of origin, such as archival documents, material culture objects, and interview data. The second major benefit of this project is the addition of resources to the highly limited pool of pedagogical materials regarding Northeast Asia. Both the monograph and the complementary website will demonstrate how the social and cultural traits of Amuria during the early modern era can be connected to preceding and following historical periods. After the end of this project, the investigator will continue to foster knowledge sharing with students and other researchers through the wiki website. 阿穆里亞地區多種族群之社會、文化交流歷史 負責人：金由美博士，歷史系助理教授，香港浸會大學 本項目的首要目標是論述阿穆裏亞近代早期（約公元1600-1910年）本地與外來人群之間的社會、文化交流歷史。「阿穆裏亞」是一個地理和文化區域，包含了中國東北的極北區域和俄羅斯西伯利亞的東南部分。這一概念本身會成為該項目重要的研究基石，它強調諸如遷徙模式和親屬關係網絡等特徵，淡化了政治邊界的重要性。此外，它還強調各個不同社區如何以阿穆爾河（黑龍江）支流來劃分邊界，同時，這些支流又成為不同社區之間的聯繫管道 。本項目亦將突出該地區多個政體和社會的共存，這不僅僅包括為數甚眾的土著民、寄居者、以及來自周邊地區的移民。這些群體之間的交流互動推動了社會和文化的協調發展，該過程反過來又影響了它們相互之間的政治、經濟關係，以及與為了統治阿穆裏亞領土而競爭的非本土國家之間的交往。通過收集所能挖掘到的史料中盡可能多的視角，本項目希望完成的研究成果是一部專著和一個維基網站。這些成果將為史學和歷史教學範例作出重要貢獻。 本項目的第一個創新之處，在於豐富了迄今尚缺乏分析的阿穆里亞本土性之概念。在分析此概念的基礎上，進一步提出了諸種通過該區域社會、政治和法律方法，決定土著人群自我識別以及外人如何看待土著地位的新因素。為此，本項目將採用考察地方歷史的研究方法，如民族學的田野調查，同時參考地方文本性和非文本性材料。研究過程將分為兩個階段。第一個階段，收集出已被版史料。第二階段，搜尋僅僅在阿穆里亞當地能夠收集到的材料，如檔案文件、物質文化物件、訪談資料等等。 本項目的第二個目的，是希望能夠對東北亞地區非常有限的教學資源進行資料補充。專著和維基網站都將顯示，阿穆里亞近代早期的社會、文化特徵與前後歷史時期的關係。該項目結束後，研究者將繼續完善相關知識，并與學生和其他研究人員通過維基網站共享研究成果。

245212.label: Realisation of objectives
245212.value: The PI achieved the first three objectives by aggregating and analyzing evidence from a variety of primary sources about the Amur River region (Amuria). The PI formulated three major categories based on quantitative and qualitative significance in order to organize the evidence: 1) religion, 2) language, and 3) material culture. Specific questions and conceptual themes were then identified for evaluating the content. The PI also presented aspects of her research for each category in several international conferences and was invited to serve as a discussant for panels about the Amur River region for two international conferences based on reputation for this research. Additionally, the PI collaborated with university colleagues to develop a digital humanities project based on a portion of the research, and to pursue a related funded project on regional cuisines in China. For the fourth objective, the PI produced three book proposals and consulted with several publishers to determine which one would make the most intellectual impact while being sufficiently marketable. Negotiations with a master cartographer to develop specialized maps for the manuscript are currently ongoing. The PI encountered major challenges to finishing the whole manuscript by the end of the grant period because of constrained access to necessary sources. A major constraint was that a majority of the texts from overseas repositories could only be acquired through the interlibrary loan system. Despite the best efforts of librarians at the PI’s home institution, there were limitations to the number of requests that could be fulfilled when no repository holding a particular text would agree to provide the loan. The PI fulfilled the fifth objective by using a newer kind of wiki platform that promotes teaching and learning as well as knowledge exchange. The wiki is designed according to the framework of the book manuscript, but will eventually be expanded to incorporate findings of the other topics examined in this project. The PI developed the wiki by teaching students in a course about Northeast China and experimenting with different ways to convey information to a broad audience while retaining intellectual value. The PI also consulted with a specialist in information science to choose an appropriate platform and to organize the featured data. The wiki currently contains selected information from the PI’s research and will be expanded upon over time. In the future, the PI will use the wiki for teaching purposes and make it available to other academics for both research and pedagogy.

245212.label: Major findings and research outcome
245212.value: Major Findings: This research generated findings in three areas: food culture and natural resources, religion, and language. Evidence analyzed about food culture and natural resources indicates that 1) the classification of “native cultures” and differentiation of traits related to material culture such as preferred foods and cuisine by the Soviet/Russian and Chinese states during the twentieth century should be critiqued and corrected more scrupulously than previous studies have attempted to do, 2) mainstream academic and popular perceptions of the Amur River region undervalue the area’s ecological diversity (although this research and some very recent publications are now revealing a decisive rectification of this attitude), 3) the main textual sources consulted for this aspect of the research reveal the invalidity of utilizing certain methodological tools such as identifying indigenous flora by Latin taxonomy and conversely, the need for more fit-for-purpose metrics for this geo-cultural area. For religion, the PI discovered the influence of the Russian Orthodox Church (ROC) in China was qualitatively significant prior to the nineteenth century, the period commonly considered as the flourishing of ROC missionary and scholarly activity, and that non-coercive interactions between representatives of the ROC and indigenous peoples in the Amur River region influenced attributes of social organization and material culture in ways that are not purely exploitative. Finally, for the impact of social and cultural interaction on language, the PI focused on the evolution of pidgins and the selection of lingua franca when two or more persons with different first languages attempted to communicate with one another. The PI learned that individuals who could be considered outsiders to the region, such as travelers or explorers, were not wholly reliant on interpreters but actually expended varying degrees of effort to learn indigenous languages. Another major finding about language is that previous studies about language usage in the region have been inappropriately skewed towards the conclusion that pidgins are all based on politically dominant languages like Russian and Chinese. By tracing how a pidgin evolves over an extended period of time, the actual composition of the language is more discernible. Research Outcome: The PI amassed a qualitatively diverse amount of data. Collecting this data led to focusing on food culture and natural resources as the subject of the book manuscript, so the relevant data about that topic will be most visible in that output. The rest of the data will be included in other future outputs.

245212.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
245212.value: The PI is presently developing all three components of this research further. To enhance the findings about religion, the PI earned a Sin Wai-Kin Junior Fellowship from the Hong Kong Institute of Humanities and Social Sciences to support research for a book manuscript about Russian Orthodoxy in China. For the food culture and natural resources aspect, the PI earned a Seed Funding grant to collect more data and also to formulate another GRF grant proposal about cultural connections between Northeast China and Southern Siberia for a future review cycle. The PI has also applied for a GRF grant during the current review cycle to build a digital onomasticon of proper nouns (personal and group names, toponyms) that can also be published in hard copy. If the proposal is successful, the PI will generate several outputs about the language-related component of this research during the next three years.

245212.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
245212.value: The Amur River region was a hub of social and cultural interaction among many populations differentiable by political allegiance but connected through economic interdependence, shared spiritual values, interest in learning and communicating through each other’s languages, and mutually influenced material culture in the early modern era. This research has generated considerable data that illustrates cooperation between groups that have been previously considered only as competitors and enemies. The findings shed new light on how this region developed characteristics that were not primarily influenced by political and economic institutions of the two imperial states that claimed it as parts of their domains. The evidence also challenges conventional and static concepts such as the division of the region into two parts as Manchuria and Siberia, and that the region’s indigenous peoples were only victims of exploitation by militarily superior peoples coming from the outside. By replacing the as-yet conventional approach of focusing on the wars and other conflicts that occurred in the region with the objective of examining how the majority of individual-to-individual or group-to-group interactions were peaceful and productive, this project contributes to the growing academic and popular interest in the social and cultural traits of river-based areas.

245212.value: In the course of conducting this research, the PI developed related projects that will facilitate knowledge transfer of historical data to present-day populations. These projects, which are still on-going, include: 1) curating a museum exhibition in Hong Kong that will open in December 2017 and present material culture of one Amur River population in a style that emphasizes the agency of those people rather than treating them as subjects or objects to be examined and judged, and will result in a compendium of chapter-length studies by leading scholars in Tungusic Studies that the PI is co-editing, and 2) aggregating data about proper nouns (personal and group names, toponyms) from throughout the Amur River region. 245512.label: Project Title(Chinese)
245512.value: 種族與歸屬之文化政治：廣州的非洲移民社區研究

245512.label: Project Objectives
245512.value: Uncover the heterogeneity of the African diaspora communities in Guangzhou Explore the multi-layered process of racial knowledge production in China’s rising market economy Compare and contrast the African diaspora experiences in China and in the United States

Explore the multi-layered process of racial knowledge production in China’s rising market economy

245512.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
245512.value: 隨著中非貿易的增長，非洲移民正在成為中國都市引人注目的群體。在過去的十年間，中國南部城市廣州迎來了大批非洲移民并形成中國最大的非洲社區，當地人稱之為巧克力城或小非洲。廣州的非洲人口主要是來自西非如尼日利亞、幾內亞、喀麥隆、利比利亞和馬裡等國家的商人和勞動者。據官方統計，自2003年以來，廣州的非洲人口以每年30-40%的速度增長。據非官方統計，目前在廣州合法居留的非洲移民有20,000人，非法移民將近200,000。廣州非洲移民的增長對於中國都市在種族、移民控管和跨文化交際方面提出了諸多緊迫的問題。2009年7月一個無身份的非洲移民為躲避中國警察檢查護照從某商貿城跳下摔死。稍後，100多名非洲人在當地派出所前舉行抗議活動。由於該事件在諸多西方媒體成為頭條新聞，關於種族主義在中國的討論一度在海內外成為爭議。本課題從比較的角度，將中國的非洲移民放在全球化和跨國遷移的大背景中研究。當今關於跨國遷移的文獻主要集中在第三世界國家向歐美發達國家移民，關於發展中國家之間移民的文獻不多。在中國的非洲移民是一個獨特的案例，因為中國在歷史上是一個移民輸出國家，並且是西方種族主義和殖民主義的受害者。本課題運用多種研究方法，探討非洲移民在廣州被接納過程中的種種矛盾現象以及他們多元化的社區建構策略。通過比較非洲移民在中國和美國的不同經歷，考察種族及種族主義在不同文化背景下意義的變遷。確切地講，本課題旨在研究關於非洲和黑色種族的知識在中國不斷发展的市場經濟中如何被建構以及這種建構對全球種族等級秩序的再生所起的作用。

245512.label: Realisation of objectives
245512.value: The PI has successfully achieved the four project objectives. The research uncovered the heterogeneity of diaspora Africans in Guangzhou in terms of nationality, language, ethnicity, gender, age, and religious beliefs. Due to the difficulty to recruit research assistants who can speak Arabic, Spanish, and Portuguese, the research did not generate any useful data on Africans who speak these languages. However, the project did cover the majority of Africans in Guangzhou, who speak either English or French. The PI finds that the formation of racial knowledge about black Africans in China is mediated by multiple internal and international factors, such as traditional Chinese aesthetic values, intersection of internal and international migration, influence of western media, and state rhetoric of Sino-African friendship. The African experience in Guangzhou differs in several ways from other parts of China. For example, Africans in Yiwu are less visible and not subjected to strict immigration control as in Guangzhou. The African diaspora experience in China is also different from that in the United States due to the temporal nature and the multiple mobility trajectories of different groups of African migrants.

245512.label: Major findings and research outcome
245512.value: The African diaspora in China is a relatively new phenomenon that is still evolving. It raises challenges to China’s immigration policy and calls for more migrant- friendly policies on the part of the Chinese state. Individual racism against black Africans has the tendency to increase due to the role of internet and popular media in spreading negative stereotypes about African migrants in Guangzhou. Epistemological racism is also a problem in China due to the continuing influence of western media, which usually contains racialized images of blacks. However, it is premature to argue for a fully developed version of institutional racism in China due to the Chinese state’s ambivalent attitudes towards issues of immigration. China is still reluctant to admit its status as an immigrant country and there is no systematic legal framework for the regulation and integration of foreign migrants in China. Although there is no institutional racism in China, there exists racial profiling among some Chinese police officers, who target black Africans for passport and visa verification. Since there is a connection between individual racism practiced by some state agents and institutional racism, there is the danger of institutional racism in China in the future. African migrants are providing business and job opportunities mainly for marginalized and disadvantaged people in China, such as migrant workers and entrepreneurs. These people have no political power to influence state policy. However, grassroots interactions between Chinese and African migrants in daily life settings may have the potential to disabuse some of the negative stereotypes against Africans. Nonetheless, due to language barrier, cultural misunderstandings, and their shared vulnerable status in urban China, mutual stereotypes and feelings of distrust are also common between Chinese and African migrants, which significantly limited the transformative power of cross-cultural business interactions. One major outcome of this project is a book manuscript, Mapping the New African Diaspora in China: Race and the Cultural Politics of Belonging, which is under contract with Routledge Press. The PI also presented the research in different regional and international conferences, and published several articles and book chapters based on this research.

245512.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
245512.value: This research is based on one specific case study, that is, African migrants in Guangzhou. In light of the increasing diversity of migrant population in China, it might be helpful to examine other foreign migrant groups such as Koreans, Vietnamese, Euro-Americans, and compare their experiences with that of African migrants. Immigration is a pressing issue that needs to be dealt with by the Chinese state. Such future project will greatly enhance our understanding of the evolution of Chinese immigration policy in terms of reception and regulation of different groups of foreign population.

245512.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
245512.value: This is an ethnographic study of African migrant experiences in Guangzhou, China. The author lived in the African community and managed to talk to both Chinese and Africans from various backgrounds. It uncovers the daily life experiences of different groups of Africans, particularly undocumented Nigerians in Guangzhou. The research is important because it treats Guangzhou as a contact zone where China’s internal migrants meet with international migrants. The author provides multiple perspectives concerning the perception of Africans in China: the central state, the local state, elite Chinese, Chinese migrant workers and small entrepreneurs. Another distinction of the project is the multi-cited nature of the research (in both China and Nigeria) and its transnational perspective. The author treats the African diaspora in Guangzhou as a dynamic community that facilitates the transnational circulation of people, good, and information between China and many African countries. The research also highlights the uniqueness of the Chinese context in the development of racial knowledge on black Africans, which is different from that in the West.

245612.label: Project Title(Chinese)
245612.value: 中國高中學生的教育過渡路徑及其社會影響﹕一項以南京市高中學生為調查對象的探索性研究

245612.label: Co - Investigator(s)
245612.value: Prof Feng, Xiaotian Dr Song, Jing Dr Wong, Odalia Ming-hung

245612.label: Project Objectives
245612.value: To explore the pathways of transition from high school to university taken by young people in urban Nanjing. To examine the effects of personal aspirations, and resources provided by family and school (cultural, social, and material) on transition pathways. To assess the impacts of different transition pathways on subsequent personal aspirations and the stock of cultural and social capital.
rows: To explore the pathways of transition from high school to university taken by young people in urban Nanjing.
To examine the effects of personal aspirations, and resources provided by family and school (cultural, social, and material) on transition pathways.
To assess the impacts of different transition pathways on subsequent personal aspirations and the stock of cultural and social capital.

245612.label: Realisation of objectives
245612.value: This project is part of the panel study which was first launched in 2010 to examine the life transitions of young people in urban Nanjing. To achieve the study objectives, a survey was conducted in 2013 on the panel of 989 respondents who were initially selected from 11 senior high schools in 2010, which span across a hierarchy of schools ranked by resource input, teaching quality, and reputation. A total of 759 respondents (at a response rate of 77%) completed a survey in 2012 that aimed to update their residential locations and activity statuses (in school or employment) after high school graduation. The 2013 survey retained 698 individuals who had participated in the previous two waves, representing 71% of the original panel. Due to the geographical dispersion of respondents, data were collected with a web survey. About 99 percent of the respondents continued education after high school graduation, more than 40% of whom went to school outside Nanjing and even overseas. The data cover the transition patterns after high school (university destinations vs. employment outcomes), social participation (extra-curricular activities and use of social media), social networks (dating and friendship ties), social capital, cultural capital, and personal aspirations. The use of web survey posed both advantages and challenges to us. While it allowed us to reach the respondents over geographical distances, the survey request could easily be ignored and we had no control over how the respondents participated and thus data quality. To overcome these problems, we have maintained regular contact with the respondents since 2010 through sending festival greetings and words of encouragement so that respondents could remember the project. In addition to economic incentives, research assistants have similar schooling and life experiences with the respondents were hired to cultivate "guanxi" with them via the social media platform prior to the survey so as to enhance cooperation and data quality. Data were linked to personal and family information collected in the baseline survey and statistical analyses were performed. The transition patterns after high school, degree of social participation, social network structure, levels of social and cultural capital were identified using the univariate analytical methods. ANOVA and regression analyses were conducted to examine the impacts of personal, family, and school factors on transition outcomes, as well as the social consequences of transition. Basic data analyses were completed but refined analyses are warranted.

245612.label: Major findings and research outcome
245612.value: Almost all the respondents (99%) reported to be enrolled in post-secondary education in 2013, and among them, 97.5% went to school in China and 60% in Nanjing. In terms of educational destinations, about 20% of the respondents attended elite universities (985 and 211 institutions) and more than 40% of the respondents attended junior colleges. Yet, our result might have overestimated the transition to higher education. Significant attrition occurred in the 2012 survey, particularly among students from one high-prestige and low-prestige high schools. Many of the “withdrawal” students from prestigious schools were later found to have gone abroad for education. Non-responding students from other schools, particularly, low-prestige schools might have left school for work because of poor university entrance examination results and felt too embarrassed to release this information to us. Further analyses show that family backgrounds make a difference in educational destinations (local vs. overseas as well as institutional prestige) but the family impact tends to be mediated by high school ranking. The findings reflect meritocratic elitism in China’s mass education, which legitimizes the intergenerational transfer of social advantages via formal education. Moreover, family origin tends to generate cumulative (dis)advantages in the educational process. Students of elite universities were more actively involved in extra-curricular activities than students of non-elite institutions. Although the family influence on activity participation is minimal, socio-economically advantaged parents were able to enrich their children’s extra-curricular experiences by sending them first to prestigious high schools and then, to elite universities. Transition to higher education generally expanded and diversified one’s social network. However, students of elite universities reported better access to social capital than students of non-elite universities. Attending elite universities yielded greater social capital benefit for students from privileged family background than for the less-privileged counterparts. Yet, participation in extra-curricular activities did help expand one’s social network and facilitated the access to social capital, particularly for the less-privileged students. Transition to higher education has also influenced other aspects of social relations. University activities and social life beyond campus were found to be important channels for developing intimate relationships. Dating partners tend to be similar in family background. Women are more likely than men to emphasize socioeconomic traits in selection of dating partners. Young people were more satisfied with their relationships with parents and communication with parents became more frequent after entering university. The project has yielded four publications, three working papers, and 11 conference presentations.

245612.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
245612.value: Since the majority of the sample in the 2013 survey consists of college/university students, the data would allow us to examine how university destinations and experiences affect the transition into the labor market. In fact, we have successfully obtained another GRF grant in 2014 with which a follow-up survey will be conducted between December 2015 and May 2016 to collect data on school-to-work transition. Further, the research team has maintained good relationship with the panel respondents in the past few years. This has enabled us to have successfully retained about 70 percent of the original sample in the 2013 survey. We can conduct further surveys to probe other life course changes of these young people. With this purpose, we plan to submit a GRF proposal in 2016 to obtain funding for another follow-up survey on the respondents’ career change, family formation, and homeownership.

245612.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
245612.value: This project, as part of the panel study on the life course transition of young people in urban China, has examined the transition to higher education among high school students in urban Nanjing. Existing studies on higher education in China have mainly focused on the attainment of university education and overall enrollment rate. Very few studies differentiate the pathways young people may take and examine their associated social factors and consequences. The project has thus filled the research gap. The empirical evidence provided by the project has illuminated the school-mediated intergenerational transmission of social (dis)advantages and the impact of school stratification on educational attainment. It has also generated four journal articles, three working papers, and 11 conference presentations. The panel data collected to date can provide the baseline information for further exploration of Chinese young people’s other life course transitions and the persistent effects of family background and school prestige on the outcomes. The data can also be used in comparative social research on educational transition and life course studies, and for student training. Lastly, the project has fostered the long-term research collaboration with Nanjing University since 2010.

247612.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
247612.value: This project is a hypermedia ethnographic study on artists’ studios in Kwun Tong industrial buildings. Recently, unaffordable property prices have become a critical issue in Hong Kong. A new East Kowloon Redevelopment Project announced in the latest Policy Address will also greatly affect the district. Hence, studying artists’ practices and their studios in Kwun Tong from the perspective of crisis and change in urban spatial contexts is essential and useful. Site/place: Prior studies have been conducted on Fotanian, Oil Street and Cattle Deport Artists Villages. The former is an organic conglomerate of artists’ studios in Fotan industrial buildings. The latter are government plans for artists to move into preservation sites. Yet, little research has been done on artists’ studios and community in Kwun Tong. Thus, a study addressing this research gap will be significant. New approaches to visual arts researches in Hong Kong: (a) Cross-disciplinary research methods – (i) research on data/statistics of rent in Kwun Tong; (ii) ethnographic research (hypermedia) (iii) structured and semi-structured interview; (iv) (con)textual analysis of artists’ works/art-making process; (v) collaborations with research subjects – artists will contribute visual/audio materials representing their studios. These subjective/personal materials will be published together with our objective/informative research output. (b) Hypermedia ethnography as a research method as well as means of presentation. Audio-visual materials do not merely assist the documentation of field notes but offer receivers ample room to experience the complex and dynamic ethnographic knowledge which cannot be fully expressed by writing alone. Recently, a few Hong Kong social scientists (Dr. Ma Kit-wai, Dr. Ho Sik-ying) conducted visual ethnographic projects with great success. This proposed research is targeted to further experiment along this trajectory of visual ethnography by applying hypermedia presentation – photographs, audio, video and hyperlinks. Aims: (i) examine why artists set up studios in Kwun Tong industrial buildings; (ii) investigate how government policies (re-vitalisation of industrial buildings and the new East Kowloon Redevelopment Project) affect artists and their practices; (iii) study what artists do in their studios; (iv) study studio set-ups; (v) explore how artists participate in and benefit from both everyday-life activities and art-events in the community; (vi) supplement existing research on artists’ studios and artists’ communities, thus generating ideas for better cultural policy. This project will produce various outcomes: (i) journal articles and conference presentations; (ii) a hypermedia ethnographic presentation on an existing locative website that is free for public access http://www.kwuntongculture.hk (Mak, 2009).

247612.label: Realisation of objectives
247612.value: All the objectives are achieved. We have visited 27 artists and designers, 25 are on and in sum 330mins of video in the web site (http://ktfactorystudio.com). They work on various media: wood work/design, leather work/design, graphic/2D design, 3D work design and production, music, music live house, fashion design/shop, photography, puppet design/production and theatre, printing, video production, hand-made guitar production, tattoo, street art, wearable and jewelleries. By interviews as well as ethnographic observation, the research shows the reasons why they set up studios and the activities they do and also their way of life. Community network and relations are also closely examined in which we realize the neighbourhood is vital to the creative cluster. Moreover, research subjects have critical comments to the revitalization policy. Last but not least, the hyper-video web site is very successful. It is a very effective way to present research findings to the general public, especially promoted on facebook (there are over 3100 likes up to Jan 2016, and over 210000 post reaches) https://www.facebook.com/ktfactorystudio/?fref=ts The web-site is selected to be featured in the data-base for interactive documentary of IDFA, International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam 2015-2016, which is the most important documentary festival in Europe. The project is also presented in conferences and a paper published in journal.

247612.label: Major findings and research outcome
247612.value: 1) Many artists/designers as major contribution for creative industries are stationed in Kwun Tong. We have visited 27 artists and designers, 25 are on and in sum 330mins of video in the web site (http://ktfactorystudio.com/). They work on various media: wood work/design, leather work/design, graphic/2D design, 3D work design and production, music, music live house, fashion design/shop, photography, puppet design/production and theatre, printing, video production, hand-made guitar production, tattoo, street art, wearable and jewelleries. They like the industrial town because of its full supply of materials (wood, papers, iron, plastic) and tools, recycled materials (wood, clothes) and tools (furniture), knowledge transfer from older generation to young folks which is a very interesting inter-generation relations, community support, community network and exchange (knowledge and ideas exchange and sharing), affordable food, easy transportation, and varieties of choices for rental space. 2) However, the research subjects are having very hard time because of the high rent. Revitalization Policy has speeded up heavy speculations on property prices and rent from 2010-2015. Sometimes, they were forced to leave and it resulted in problems of sustainability. There are double up rent in some cases. 8 out of the 27 artists/designers we visited have moved out of their studio during the research time (2012-2015), or even out of Kwun Tong area. 3) All research subjects have negative comments to the revitalization policy of industrial buildings. Government needs to further understand the situation of creative industries in the following ways for better policy: a) Downplaying Kwun Tong as an industrial town and make it the past is wrong. Creative industries need support from the community of industrial town in terms of materials and tools, knowledge and craft. Government needs to relearn the idea of industry, that is not the old ones but creative industries. Industries are NOT the past but present. b) They need space in factory buildings but NOT those in offices to work. They need workshop space for dirty works and storage. Offices are NOT good for them. c) Factory space are in great demand, they are NOT vacant. If the government wants to develop and support creative industry, they should keep factory buildings, rework on the regulations/laws regarding land use and fire safety, but not to destroy them and replaced by offices and hotels. This only results in speculations of property prices and further put creative industries into a more difficult position.

247612.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
247612.value: It is important to go on looking at the development of the creative industries in the area. It is because the government has announced the end of the revitalization policy in 2016. It will be a good follow up to know more the ways of life and the studios of the artists and designers when the speculations stops and also during the downside of the property market. It is also good to further study whether the creative cluster has grown or not after the policy. Lastly, it is important to follow up whether the government will do anything to really help the creative industries by reworking the regulations and laws on the usage of factory buildings. Without doing these things, it is NOT genuine help and support to the creative industries.

247612.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
247612.value: This is a research-creative project, in which both the topic of research and ways of presenting research findings are key subjects. Regarding topic of research, unaffordable property price and a shortage of space have long been critical issues in Hong Kong. It is a disturbing problem affecting many Hong Kong citizens, especially artists/designers in Kwun Tong area facing the Revitalization Policy since 2010. Doing ethnographic study to the ways artists/designers survive and set up studios in factory buildings is needed, meaningful and important. The research (with ethnographic video on an interactive web-based platform) shows in details the vibrant community of creative industries experiencing difficulties to survive because of high rent and lack of support from the Government. However, they have been trying to live on their own, building up the community network, their businesses and various types of activities that shape the unique landscape in Kwun Tong industrial town. The research findings are presented on a hyper-video web-site, From The Factory (http://ktfactorystudio.com) which is free for public access. It is promoted on facebook for further reach out to various sectors of people from and outside Kwun Tong Community.

247912.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
247912.value: Ensuring young people are steered on a path to healthy adulthood is regarded as one of the main goals of successful development during adolescence (Adams, 2000). However, due to profound social and economic changes, young people’s transition to adulthood is often delayed. The five traditional markers for entering adulthood, such as leaving the parental home, finishing university, getting a first job, marriage or becoming a parent (Arnett, 2004) are no longer applicable. Instead, the concept of Emerging Adulthood (EA) for young people aged 18-25 has been proposed as a new period of human development in various different countries (see for example Arnett, 2007; Buhl & Lanz, 2007; Nelson, Bager & Wu, 2004). In Hong Kong, approximately 0.7 million people (around 10% of the total population) fall into the 18-25 age bracket each year (Census and Statistics Department [CSD], 2010) and are expected to make a successful transition to adult life (Catan, 2004). However, there is dissent among this group of young people, who have been labelled as “a lost generation”, “never growing up”, (Lam, 2007), “not currently in employment, education or training (NEETs), and “otaku boys and girls” (people who are always at home playing on the Internet). Are these people emerging adults or are they in crisis? What does adulthood mean to these emerging adults in Hong Kong? Surprisingly, there is very little local research about the concepts and experiences of young people making the transition to adulthood and the notion of EA in the Hong Kong context.. Using an exploratory, sequential mixed-methods research design, the purpose of this study is to examine EA among young people (aged 18-25) in Hong Kong. It comprises two parts. Firstly, a quantitative study using the Hong Kong Chinese Emerging Adulthood Scale (CEAS-HK), based on a 143-item questionnaire developed by Arnett (1997), will be administered to 2,000 young people (including both students and non-students) to explore the criteria for EA, its magnitude and the factors affecting it. Secondly, a qualitative study involving 10 focus groups will be conducted with 40 participants from the quantitative study to explore their subjective experiences of transitioning to adulthood. By using these two approaches, the study aims to gain a better understanding of EA in Hong Kong, which may help to develop a positive youth policy and design relevant services to help emerging adults cope with the challenges of contemporary Hong Kong. 摘要 能否發展成為一個健康的成人是每個青少年需要面對的重要發展任務（Adams，2000）。然而，由於日新月異的社會發展與變化，青少年發展成為成人的過程普遍延長。傳統的成人標準，如離開父母獨立生活、完成大學教育、擁有第一份工作、結婚或為人父母（Arnett，2004），顯然已經不合時宜，無法用以衡量當代青少年的發展狀況。因此，阿納特（Arnett）提出的“成人過渡期”（“準成人”）（Emerging Adulthood）用以描述年齡為18－25歲之間的年輕人發展階段，此概念為不同國家的研究者所採用並得到論證。準成人階段也逐漸被認為是人類發展中的一個新階段。 在香港，每年約有70萬年齡為18－25歲之間的年輕人，約占總人口的10％（香港統計處，2012）。這一代的年輕人經常被標簽為“沒有長大的一代”（Lam, 2007），或“宅男宅女”。那麼，他們是處於成人的過渡期，還是陷於發展的危機（埃裡克森語）？對他們而言，成人到底是什麼概念，成人的標準是什麼呢？雖然不同國家或地區學者對新生一代成人的概念和標準進行不同的研究，但是在香港類似的研究還很匱乏。 是次研究是一種探索性研究，結合量化與質性研究的優勢設計此研究，旨在探索在香港年齡為18－25的年輕人對準成人概念的理解以及他們在成長過程中可能遇到的挑戰是什麼。本次研究分為兩個部分，第一個部分為量化研究，應用含有143條問題的香港版的準成人量表（CEAS-HK），邀請2000此年齡段的年輕人（包括學生和非學生）參與本次的問卷調查，以探索年輕人“準成人”的標準，對他們的重要性，以及其影響因素。第二個部分則採用質性研究方法，邀請40位合資格的年輕人參與聚焦小組的訪談（每4人一組，共10組），瞭解他們自身對過度發展為成人過程中的感受與體會，以探索他們在此過程中所面臨的挑戰。通過是次的研究，研究者希望更好地瞭解香港“準成人”的狀況以及他們所面臨的各種挑戰，以促進政府發展配套的青年政策，提供更好青年服務，以協助他們更好地應對發展過程要面對的挑戰。

247912.label: Realisation of objectives
247912.value: Objective 1 - To outline the profile of emerging adults, and to establish a set of criteria for Hong Kong emerging adults: In order to outline the profile of emerging adults in Hong Kong, to develop and validate a Chinese Emerging Adulthood Scale (CEAS-HK) by exploring its cultural dimensionality in Hong Kong, a total number of 2660 young people were invited to participate in a series of studies. These include, a preliminary study (101 young people), a pre-pilot study (384 young people), a pilot study (471 young people), a main study (1704 young poeple) from different sectors, as well as 7 focus groups with 45 young persons after the main study. The CEAS-HK is confirmed with good validity and reliability as supported by Exploratory Factor Analysis with a 7-factor model that explained 53.63% of the total variance. The 7 factors consist of (1) relational capacities, (2) bio-social maturity, (3) family capacities, (4) norm compliance, (5) independency, (6) capacity for intimacy and (7) legal translation. The factor of ‘relational capacities’ was a newly emerged factors in the alternative factor structure of CEAS-HK which differed in the previous studies the original seven factors model of (Arnett, 1998, 2001, 2003). It reflects the cultural characteristic in conceptualization of adulthood that most participants endorsed characteristics of adulthood relating to one’s relational qualities and signifies the theme of interdependency. Objective 2 - To identify how EA may vary as a function of socio-demographic factors: In order to examine the influence the socio-demographic factors on the development of emerging adults, a sample of 1704 young people, which included 738 male (43.3%), 961 female (56.4%) (5 missing, 0.3%), aged 18 to 29 years old (M= 20.95, SD= 2.42), was recruited from the online questionnaire system, secondary schools, universities, vocational education institutes, community colleges, non-profit organisations, social services centres and general public in Hong Kong. However, response rate from social service sectors in recruiting respondents with NEET status was unsatisfactorily, even after a period of extension of data collection. To improve with this inadequacy, various qualitative interviews had been conducted with young people of NEET. Results from these interviews showed that the more advantaged groups of emerging adults (e.g. degree students) mostly experienced extended participation in education and occupational advancement. Moreover, with the education qualification obtained, it would be more possible for them to move upward socially. On contrary, those participants from less advantage groups (e.g. NEET), they were caught at the bottom end of the social scale, hardly finding a direction to be able to move upward. The gap between these two groups of emerging adults has been widening as our society becomes more information-based with scarcity of high-paying job in other industrial sectors. Participants found it hard to find jobs that could fit their talents and expectations reasonably in view of the absence of sufficient training alternatives. Objective 3 - To collect the subjective experiences of emerging adults and to identify the impact of EA on different aspects of their development: Since the nature and the concept of adulthood has been transforming, to understanding the impact of culture and social values on subjective perception of emerging adulthood in the eyes of young people, 7 focus groups (N=45) had also been conducted to examine the subjective experiences of individuals. The qualitative interviews have identified subjective experiences from young people on how they perceived important criteria that deemed necessarily to adulthood, as well as the impacts on them. Objective 4 - To provide empirical evidence, adn construct a database, of the characteristics and needs of emerging adults that can inform research and enhance practice and policymaking: Results from quantitative study showed that there was a considerable percentage (55.4%) of 18-29 years old respondents chose the ambiguous response “in some respects yes, in some respects no” when they were asked if they have reached adulthood. This finding indicates that there is a notable portion of young people who have a sense of ambivalence about their own adult status. It also suggested that emerging adulthood may be a transitional period of development that is experienced by young people in Hong Kong. In addition, this sense of ambivalence varied in degree between younger (18-23 years old) and older emerging adults (24-29 years old). The older group achieved a stronger sense of adulthood compared with younger group, indicating a progressive change in the differentiation process within this developmental period. Drawing upon the qualitative interviews, age was regarded as a catalytic agent as participants believed that maturity comes with life experience that allows them to grow, and more importantly, to have personal reflection. Finally yet importantly, this study has identified areas for further research and policy suggestions. First, further development and validation of assessment tools (e.g. The IDEA: Inventory of the Dimensions of Emerging Adulthood) in understanding the features of emerging adulthood is needed. It may be helpful to examine those features of emerging adulthood in relation to the optimal development and well-beings of emerging adults that could inform future policy, education and social service development. Moreover, future study on emerging adults’ relationships with their families, peers and romantic partners is suggested as to examine their developmental trajectories in a relational contexts. The newly identified factor ‘relational capacities’ highlighted the cultural distinctness of the meaning of adulthood in the Hong Kong context. Participants endorsed characteristics relating to relational qualities and interdependency in defining their adult status, such as ‘to learn always to have good control of your emotions’ and ‘to be able affirm his/her own value’ etc. This involves a reciprocal process for emerging adults to define themselves in relation to significant others. As highlighted in the factor of ‘independency’, the ability for emerging adults to develop their independence and assume their responsibilities was linked to the parents’ ability to be emotionally differentiated with their emerging adult children and to allow them to function adequately based on their real ability and needs in order to take on their adult roles. In addition, future research of emerging adulthood should include sample from a wider background (e.g. juvenile) to minimize any impact related to the idiosyncrasies in a particular sample. Besides, futher studies may replicate the present findings in order to provide feedback on the stability and generalizability of the CEAS-HK.

247912.label: Major findings and research outcome
247912.value: First, the present study has made a significant contribution to the development and validation of CEAS-HK which possess good psychometric properties to use in understanding an unprecedented phenomenon of emerging adulthood in local Hong Kong context. Second, qualitative study had been conducted to offer insights into this developmental period and to enhance the sensitivity of indigenous measurement by taking consideration of the cultural and contextual factors. Third, a new factor structure of ‘relational capacity’ represented a critical component of CEAS-HK that highlighted the cultural uniqueness regarding the meaning of adulthood amongst Hong Kong emerging adults. As highlighted in the factor of ‘independency’, the ability for emerging adults to develop their independency and assume their responsibilities was linked to the parents’ ability to be emotionally differentiated with their emerging adult children and to allow them to function adequately based on their real ability and needs in order to take on their adult roles. Extended departure to adulthood has significant influences in future social services and policy for young people. Several common structural obstacles as revealed in the qualitative study, including unaffordable housing market, limited vocational choices, and high structural demands of existing educational systems etc., represented the major struggles for Hong Kong emerging adults to launch and achieve their independence. At the same time, families may have to extend support to their emerging adult children.

247912.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
247912.value: The present study has made a significant contribution to the study of emerging adulthood in local Chinese Hong Kong context. However, this study has certain limitations due to our sampling. Although a cluster sampling method was employed, response rate from social service sectors in recruiting respondents with NEET status was unsatisfactorily, even after a period of extension of data collection. Future studies may replicate the present findings in order to provide feedback on the stability and generalizability of the CEAS-HK. Besides, this study does not take into account the diversity that exists within families. Future work needs to take into account the diversity of various structural and socio-demographic factors of families in the beliefs concerning criteria for adulthood. Moreover, longitudinal research is recommended to help locate social and psychological factors that contributed to the emerging process of young people moving to adulthood.

247912.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
247912.value: Since there is a paucity of study on emerging adulthood in Hong Kong Chinese population, a series of studies were conducted to contribute a more comprehensive understanding of the conception of emerging adulthood and the developmental needs of emerging adults in Hong Kong through a construction and validation of the Chinese version of Emerging Adulthood Scale – Hong Kong (CEAS-HK). A sequential explanatory mixed-method design was employed in this research with a total sample of 2576 young people aged 18-29 in Hong Kong. Some significant findings were identified from the present study regarding the psychometric properties of CEAS-HK and the cultural heterogeneity of emerging adulthood in Hong Kong. First, the findings of validation study revealed that the CEAS-HK has good psychometric properties with its use with young people in the Hong Kong context. Second, there was a notable portion of emerging adults who have a sense of ambivalence about their own adult status. Third, some traditional demographic markers (such as getting married, becoming a parent and completing study) were found to be less significant in determining one’s adult status. The focus group interviews in the second stage provided a qualitative account of emerging adults’ subjective and psychological experiences of transition.

248812.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
248812.value: 當今中國煙草消費總量常居世界之冠，許多人由於吸煙致死，公眾健康與衛生面臨嚴峻挑戰 (Gu, Kelly, et al., 2009)。據預測，三十年之內,中國三分之一的青少男性會因吸煙致死 (The Epoch Times, 2004)。最近調查顯示，年紀最小的煙民為14歲，比1997年的最小年齡年輕了5歲；低齡煙民比例自1997年以來持續上漲 (WHO, 2002)。因此，中國應主要致力於防止年輕群體，特別是青少年男性的吸煙行為。1996年全國普查顯示只有約六分之一煙民嘗試戒煙，而成功戒煙的比例則更小。大部分(83%)的煙民根本無意戒菸 (Chinese Academy of Preventive Medicine, 1997).這顯示吸煙行為一旦開始就很難戒掉，因此防患於未然顯得更加必要。 在中國, 男性開始吸煙的年齡主要介於16到20歲之間 (Wang, Borland, & Whelan, 2005)，並且多數由實驗性的社交群體吸煙行為開始 (Kang, 1992)。事實上,大多數人的吸煙習慣是在青少年同伴、同事與朋友的影響下開始的 (Committee on Youth Smoking Prevention, 2010)。要有效地防止吸煙，應首先教育年輕人自覺抵制吸煙同伴的影響；而這一能力的形成與強化，關鍵在於找出拒煙的困難和因時致宜的溝通策略。 本專案將應用焦點小組討論研究方法，以典型的勸煙行為為研究範本，探索中國青少年在拒絕勸煙的情況下所面對的文化、社會、人際、心理上的諸多挑戰，並提出有效、合情理的拒煙策略。根據此焦點小組的發現，我們會針對不同情況提出一系列拒絕勸煙的相關策略。之後，我們會做民調以探求以上策略的有效性與適用性。本項目的成果將為減少中國青少年吸煙的人際干預提供理論及現實基礎，從而促進青少年吸煙防控策略的形成。

248812.label: Major findings and research outcome
248812.value: Findings from Paper 1 – “Focus Group Findings of Smoking Onset among Male Youth in China” Home and school anchored a large number of early smoking activities, and, particularly, teenagers considered school toilets and dorms safe havens for smoking. Many participants smoked first cigarettes offered by peers and others during social interactions and some smoked on their own. Objects of teenagers’ curiosity consisted of attributes of cigarette products, smoking techniques, and physical reactions. More participants disclosed negative first smoking experiences than those reporting positive reactions. Negative first physical experience motivated some participants to acquire better smoking techniques. Cigarette offers induced reciprocal offers, exacerbating smoking experimentation. Heavy experimentation occurred before graduation from high school. The current findings call for school-based and home-based antismoking interventions. Findings from Paper 2 –“Cigarette Initiation among Chinese Male Teenagers in Early Smoking Interactions” Group discussions indicated a high prevalence of cigarette initiation among peers, and such initiation often translated into immediate smoking. Of the identified cigarette initiation appeals, “face” and normative pressure appeals were the most difficult to reject. Upon first initiation attempts, more teenagers accepted cigarettes than rejected them. Reasons for both cigarette initiation and acceptance served primarily to facilitate social interaction. Upon rejections, initiating teenagers (agents) who insisted on the smoking requests often gained compliance. Profiles of peer agents were constructed. Key practical implications point to prioritized efforts in reducing cigarette initiation and simultaneously enhancing refusal efficacy. Findings from Paper 3 – “Chinese Male Adolescents Resisting Cigarettes from Peers: Tactics, Perceptions, and Contextual Characteristics” Nonconfrontational refusal tactics were frequently used. Of the nine identified cigarette refusal categories, consistent and firm declaration of the non-smoking status was considered most effective. Upon rejections, majority of those offering cigarettes made no further attempts. Most participants held neutral attitudes toward refusals rather than a pervasive disliking assumed in the literature. Conclusion: Health communicators and educators can enhance Chinese male adolescents’ cigarette refusal efficacy by instilling refusal confidence with information of general neutral attitudes toward refusal and high refusal response efficacy and by training them to choose appropriate refusal tactics. Findings from Paper 4, “A Survey of Cigarette Initiation among Male Teenagers in China,” is still in progress. Constructed based on the findings from the focus group interviews, this survey reports (a) high prevalence of cigarette initiation (b) the identification of appropriate and effective cigarette rejection tactics, and (c) several developed scales such as Cigarette Initiation Tendency and Cigarette Refusal Efficacy.

248812.label: Potential for further development of the research and the proposed course of action
248812.value: The current findings can lead to three research projects. A GRF proposal has been submitted for Project 1. Upon completion of Project 1, Projects 2 & 3 will be pursued. We discovered that several normative influences exert impact on teenagers’ cigarette initiation and smoking. Yet the nature of qualitative studies does not allow us to test the relative strengths of these influences. Project 1 seeks to conduct a meta-synthesis and a meta-analysis that systematically review norm-based empirical research and compares the existing theoretical frameworks of social norms and provide a basis for us to choose/enact an appropriate framework for our norm-based antismoking research. Guided by the framework from Project 1, Project 2 features an experiment that tests the relative strengths of normative influences on male Chinese teenagers’ smoking. In Project 3, we will use the current findings to enact an intervention program that includes informing students of the negative perceptions of cigarette initiation and teaching students cigarette refusal communication. We then identify two comparable high schools in China through a baseline study. Having executing the intervention program in one school for semester, we will test smoking incidence at both schools for comparison to see if the intervention program is effective.

248812.label: Layman's Summary ofCompletion Report
248812.value: Despite an abundance of research on cigarette smoking in China, little has been done to examine cigarette initiation as the trigger and sustainer of smoking among Chinese teenagers. We conducted this focus group study to discover how teenagers interact in cigarette smoking situations. Particularly, we discovered that male teenagers offered each other cigarettes and exacerbated smoking experimentation. They often were afraid of rejecting cigarette offers for fear of being disliked. In discussing cigarette refusal tactics, some preferred to use nonconfrontational refusal tactics, others suggested firm and consistent declarations of the non-smoking status. Thus, health communicators and educators can enhance Chinese male adolescents’ cigarette refusal efficacy by instilling refusal confidence with information of general neutral attitudes toward refusal and high refusal success rate and by training them to choose appropriate refusal tactics. The findings can be used for designing antismoking intervention/education materials and programs that discourage cigarette initiation and teach and train cigarette-refusal communication skills. Such education materials include video segments, brochures, and interactive websites. In the end, we hope that teenagers exposed to our research-based interventions will reduce cigarette initiation, increase cigarette refusal, and lower cigarette intake among Chinese teenagers.

249612.label: Project Title(Chinese)
249612.value: 折獄安民:晚明(1550–1645)判牘所反映的東南沿海社會秩序管理經驗

249612.label: Project Objectives
249612.value: To investigate and evaluate the legislative, judicial and educational means conceived to maintain social stability, if not to build a “harmonious society”, in the commercialized south-east China coastal area by studying the judicial mechanisms employed and the actions taken by frontline officials. To pay particular attention to how marginal social groups were identified and managed so as to keep order in these coastal societies. To provide an analysis that may help understand similar issues in modern China, as a piece of original research that uses case studies to examine the lower echelons of society as well as the judicial apparatus. To add new dimensions to existing regional studies of China in the sixteenth to seventeenth centuries, especially those relevant to the economically-prosperous but politically-peripheral southeast provinces such as Jiangsu, Zhejiang, Fujian and Guangdong (influenced by the “Japanese pirates” and the growth of international trade networks for more than two centuries under Ming rule). To build a framework of electronic database of court cases from the late-Ming era which plays the role of index to these underestimated materials and facilitates future input of the text of cases when further research funds are secured.

249612.label: Abstract as per original application (English/Chinese)
249612.value: This study explores how social order was maintained by the Ming regime (1368-1645) in south-east China during the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries, in the light of cases tried by local judges. By examining these documented legal cases, the study seeks to identify the security challenges, particularly the management of discriminated-against social groups such as mariners, foreigners, bondservants, prostitutes, homosexuals and wandering beggars, in the south-eastern provinces where international and domestic trade flourished. In doing so it also explores the conceptions of maintaining local security proposed by frontline officials in a rapidly-growing economy. Through a deep understanding of the crimes and realities of local communities in the late-Ming and early-Qing regimes on the south China coast, and by building an electronic database of all the available late-Ming court cases, the study aims to contribute to social and legal studies of traditional China, propose ideas for confronting similar problems in contemporary Chinese society, and contribute generally to research on problems of social control. 本研究以前線司法官員的判牘為主要資料, 探討晚明(1550–1645)政府如何維持東南沿海的社會秩序。透過分析那些存世案件的內容, 我們將深入研究經濟繁盛的東南省分, 在治安上所面對的挑戰, 其中特別注意有關海員、番夷、奴婢、娼妓、同性戀者及流丐等社會邊緣人士的管治。與此同時, 我們亦會分析臨民官員對這個世變中的晚明社會有何管治理念。透過深入理解晚明的罪行及地方社會實況, 並以電子數據庫分析相關判牘資料, 本研究將對中國社會史及法制史研究作出貢獻, 並為當代中國社會在處理類似問題時, 提供歷史的借鑑經驗, 同時也為社會秩序方面的研究提供新的線索。

249612.label: Realisation of objectives
249612.value: The relatively short duration of the project (24 months) made the full realisation of the project’s objective, building a comprehensive electronic database of late Ming judicial cases, unrealistic. The project did build a framework for such a database, which can be expanded into a comprehensive database in the future, when more human and financial resources are secured. As a pilot project, the Principal Investigator analysed representative casebooks from the late Ming period and, in collaboration with an international team of scholars sharing similar interests, built a preliminary database for analysing spatial and jurisprudential information from casebooks from Ming and Qing China. The other qualitative research objectives were all satisfactorily achieved. The Principal Investigator published a dozen journal articles and conference papers, addressing all of the issues raised in the original application. First, the legal principles and judicial mechanisms of Ming China were discussed in five papers focused on the roots of social disorder in the Southeast Coast. Specifically, the five papers discussed the ‘harsh’ punishments in the Ming judicial system, the uniqueness of the Ming judicial system, judicial torture in the late Ming and early Qing periods, local prisons in the late Ming Canton, and the forensic knowledge of Ming legal scholars, respectively. In addition, a conference paper consisting of a literature review of studies of Ming casebooks was presented to encourage future research in this field. Second, the research outputs included studies of marginal social groups such as sailors, ethnic minorities, foreigners and social outcasts. Although they have not yet been published, papers directly addressing some other marginal social groups, namely, prostitutes, beggars, homosexuals and yamen runners are currently under preparation. Third, some of the issues discussed in this project, such as legal principles for dealing with marginal social groups, problems in fact-finding methods and prison management, and the corruption of the police force, are highly relevant to modern China. The project could shed light on solutions to these problems by identifying some historical, cultural and institutional reasons for bad judicial management in the Chinese context. Finally, the regional characteristics of the coastal provinces reflected in the casebooks, such as the maritime transportation network of the Zhujiang Delta area, were seminally investigated by this project.
